Chapter 1 · Step-by-step

Purification and Characterisation of Organic Compounds

Crystallisation to chromatography, Lassaigne tests and quantitative estimations.

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

Purification
1. Purification techniques2. Crystallization3. Sublimation4. Distillation5. Differential extraction6. Chromatography
Qualitative Analysis
7. Qualitative analysis8. Detection of extra elements9. Nitrogen10. Sulphur11. Phosphorus12. Halogens
Quantitative Analysis
13. Quantitative analysis14. Estimation of carbon15. Estimation of hydrogen16. Estimation of nitrogen17. Estimation of halogens18. Estimation of sulphur19. Estimation of phosphorus20. Calculation of empirical formula21. Calculation of molecular formula22. Organic quantitative analysis

Deep Dive · Purify, identify, quantify

Purification sorts by property gaps (crystallisation solubility, sublimation vapour pressure, distillation boiling points, extraction partition, chromatography adsorption) checked by melting-boiling constancy; qualitative Lassaigne fusion converts covalent N/S/X to ions (Prussian blue, nitroprusside violet, silver precipitates; phosphorus via molybdate yellow); quantitative combustion-Kjeldahl-Dumas-Carius methods weigh products into percentages, empirical ratios and molecular multiples. Purify first (melting constancy proves), identify elements second, quantify third - analysis in strict order.
NEET facts:
  • Lassaigne: N blue (Prussian), S violet (nitroprusside), X white/yellow silver precipitates.
  • Kjeldahl misses nitro/azo nitrogen; empirical needs percentages, molecular needs molar mass.
Fig: Purify first, identify elements second, weigh percentages third - analysis order.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Lassaigne test for nitrogen gives colour

Solution: Sodium cyanide plus iron salts make ferriferrocyanide blue.

Chapter 1 · Topic 1

Purification techniques

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCPurificationStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Purification of organic compounds (Purification & Characterisation, topic 1/20) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$NaX+AgNO_3\\to AgX\\downarrow$ (white AgCl, cream AgBr, yellow AgI); $R_f=d_{sample}/d_{solvent}$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Purification of organic compounds” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Explanation

Concept. Chromatography (Purification & Characterisation, topic 8/20) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$NaX+AgNO_3\\to AgX\\downarrow$ (white AgCl, cream AgBr, yellow AgI); $R_f=d_{sample}/d_{solvent}$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Chapter 1 · Topic 7

Qualitative analysis

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQualitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Qualitative analysis finds which elements and groups a compound holds: Lassaigne sodium-fusion converts covalent N, S, halogens into ionic salts (NaCN, Na2S, NaX) detectable by classic tests (Prussian blue for N, violet nitroprusside for S, AgNO3 precipitates for halogens). Functional-group tests (unsaturation, alcohol, carbonyl, acid, amine) then narrow identity. Qualitative answers WHAT is present; quantitative measures HOW MUCH - analysis in that order always.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lassaigne fusion converts covalent elements to detectable ions.
  • Qualitative (what) precedes quantitative (how much).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Lassaigne test fuses organic compounds with metal

Solution: Sodium fusion converts N/S/X to ionic cyanide, sulphide and halides.
Example 1.

Q. An organic liquid is suspected to contain nitrogen, sulphur or halogens. Outline the qualitative analysis sequence.

  1. Fuse a pea-sized sample with dry sodium in an ignition tube, plunge into distilled water, boil and filter - the Lassaigne extract.
  2. Test one part with FeSO4 + FeCl3 (Prussian blue = N), second part with sodium nitroprusside (violet = S), third acidified part with AgNO3 (precipitate = halogens).
  3. If N and S both present, expect blood-red ferric thiocyanate instead of pure blue.

Answer: Lassaigne fusion first, then blue (N), violet (S), silver precipitate (X) tests in order.

Chapter 1 · Topic 11

Phosphorus

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQualitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phosphorus detection (Lassaigne extract oxidised with sodium peroxide fusing to phosphate, then ammonium molybdate test) gives yellow ammonium phosphomolybdate precipitate. Phosphorus rarely examined alone - usually alongside N/S/halogen panels in unknown analysis. Correct oxidation (peroxide fusion, not plain heating) is essential; incomplete oxidation misses phosphate entirely. Yellow precipitate diagnoses phosphorus decisively.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Peroxide fusion to phosphate, then yellow molybdate precipitate.
  • Incomplete oxidation misses phosphate - fuse thoroughly.
Remember
  • Yellow ammonium phosphomolybdate proves phosphorus.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Phosphorus in organic compounds is detected after fusion as

Solution: Oxidised phosphate plus molybdate yields diagnostic yellow.
Example 1.

Q. How is phosphorus detected in an organic compound? Give the chemistry.

  1. Fuse the compound with sodium peroxide (oxidises all P to phosphate) and extract with water.
  2. Add concentrated HNO3 and ammonium molybdate, warm gently.
  3. Yellow precipitate of ammonium phosphomolybdate confirms phosphorus.

Answer: Peroxide fusion to phosphate, then yellow molybdate precipitate proves P.

Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 1 · Topic 13

Quantitative analysis

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Quantitative analysis measures element percentages: Liebig combustion (C to CO2, H to H2O weighed), Kjeldahl/Dumas (N to ammonia/nitrogen gas), Carius (halogens/S/P to silver halides, BaSO4, phosphomolybdate precipitates weighed). From percentages come empirical formulas (simplest ratios), from molar mass comes molecular formula (empirical multiple). Estimation methods are gravimetric/volumetric classics - weigh products, compute backwards.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Combustion (C/H), Kjeldahl-Dumas (N), Carius (X/S/P) estimate elements.
  • Percentages give empirical; molar mass gives molecular formula.
Estimation methods
PointDetail
C, HLiebig combustion to CO2/H2O
NKjeldahl (ammonia) / Dumas (N2 gas)
X, S, PCarius (AgX, BaSO4, molybdate)
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Nitrogen estimation by Kjeldahl converts nitrogen to

Solution: Digested ammonia distilled into acid then back-titrated.
Example 1.

Q. 0.40 g of an organic compound gave 0.88 g CO2 and 0.36 g H2O on combustion. Find C and H percentages.

  1. C mass = 12/44 × 0.88 = 0.24 g; %C = 0.24/0.40 × 100 = 60%.
  2. H mass = 2/18 × 0.36 = 0.04 g; %H = 0.04/0.40 × 100 = 10%.
  3. Remainder 30% is oxygen by difference (if only C, H, O present).

Answer: %C = 60%, %H = 10% (Liebig combustion ratios 12/44 and 2/18).

Chapter 1 · Topic 14

Estimation of carbon

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Carbon estimation (Liebig combustion: weighed sample burnt in oxygen, CO2 absorbed in KOH tubes, mass gain gives carbon via 12/44 ratio) typically yields ~69 percent for glucose-class compounds. Dry oxygen flow, complete combustion (no CO/soot), pre-weighed absorption tubes and blank corrections ensure accuracy. Percentage C = 12/44 × (CO2 mass/sample mass) × 100 - ratio arithmetic every estimation shares.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Combustion to CO2 weighed in KOH tubes; 12/44 ratio gives C.
  • Complete burning plus blank correction ensure accuracy.
Remember
  • 12/44 converts CO2 mass to carbon mass.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

In Liebig combustion, CO2 produced is absorbed in

Solution: Potash bulbs trap CO2; mass gain measures carbon.
Example 1.

Q. In an estimation, 0.25 g compound gave 0.55 g CO2. Calculate %C. Why is a blank correction needed?

  1. C mass = 12/44 × 0.55 = 0.15 g; %C = 0.15/0.25 × 100 = 60%.
  2. Blank run (no sample) measures CO2 from reagents/air; subtract it so only sample carbon counts.
  3. Incomplete combustion (CO/soot) would under-read carbon.

Answer: %C = 60%; blank correction removes background CO2 error.

Chapter 1 · Topic 15

Estimation of hydrogen

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Hydrogen estimation (same Liebig combustion: water absorbed in CaCl2 tubes, mass gain gives hydrogen via 2/18 ratio) runs alongside carbon in one burning - CO2 and H2O tubes in series weigh both elements together. Anhydrous CaCl2 (or Mg(ClO4)2) traps water quantitatively; percentage H = 2/18 × (H2O mass/sample) × 100. Dry apparatus matters - stray moisture inflates hydrogen values.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Water trapped in CaCl2 tubes; 2/18 ratio gives H.
  • One combustion weighs C and H together in series.
Remember
  • 2/18 converts water mass to hydrogen mass.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Water from combustion is absorbed for hydrogen estimation in tubes of

Solution: Calcium chloride traps water; mass gain measures hydrogen.
Example 1.

Q. 0.30 g compound gave 0.27 g H2O. Find %H. What error does moist apparatus cause?

  1. H mass = 2/18 × 0.27 = 0.03 g; %H = 0.03/0.30 × 100 = 10%.
  2. Moist CaCl2 tubes or humid air add stray water, inflating H values.
  3. Dry apparatus plus guard tubes keep water measurement honest.

Answer: %H = 10%; stray moisture over-reads hydrogen - dry everything.

Chapter 1 · Topic 16

Estimation of nitrogen

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nitrogen estimation splits two classics: Kjeldahl (conc. H2SO4 digestion converts N to ammonium sulphate - nitro/azo/diazo groups excluded - then NaOH liberates ammonia distilled into standard acid, back-titrated) for most compounds, Dumas (CuO combustion to N2 gas measured volumetrically over KOH absorbing CO2) universally including nitro groups. Kjeldahl suits labs (no gas handling); Dumas suits all nitrogen types.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Kjeldahl: digest to ammonia, distil, titrate (not nitro/azo).
  • Dumas: combust to N2 gas measured over KOH.
Nitrogen methods
PointDetail
KjeldahlH2SO4 digest, NH3 distil-titrate; excludes nitro/azo
DumasCuO burn to N2 gas over KOH; universal
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Kjeldahl method CANNOT estimate nitrogen in compounds containing

Solution: Oxidised nitrogen resists sulphuric-acid digestion to ammonia.
Example 1.

Q. 0.50 g of an amine gave ammonia requiring 10 mL of 1M HCl in a Kjeldahl estimation. Find %N.

  1. Moles HCl = 1 × 10/1000 = 0.01 = moles NH3 = moles N.
  2. N mass = 0.01 × 14 = 0.14 g; %N = 0.14/0.50 × 100 = 28%.
  3. Shortcut: %N = 1.4 × N_acid × V(mL) / sample(g) = 1.4 × 1 × 10/0.5 = 28%.

Answer: %N = 28% (Kjeldahl shortcut 1.4NV/w).

Example 2.

Q. Why does Kjeldahl fail for nitrobenzene but Dumas works?

  1. Kjeldahl H2SO4 digestion cannot reduce -NO2 nitrogen to ammonia.
  2. Dumas CuO combustion oxidises ALL nitrogen to N2 gas measured over KOH.
  3. Choose Dumas for nitro, azo and diazo compounds.

Answer: Kjeldahl misses oxidised nitrogen; Dumas combusts everything to N2.

Chapter 1 · Topic 17

Estimation of halogens

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Halogen estimation (Carius: fuming HNO3 plus AgNO3 in sealed tubes oxidises X to AgX precipitate weighed - Cl/Br/I as AgCl/AgBr/AgI via Ag/X mass ratios) handles all halogens quantitatively. Sealed-tube heating (pressure digestion) ensures complete oxidation; gravimetric weighing gives precision. Percentage X = (AgX mass × X/AgX ratio / sample) × 100 - precipitate arithmetic standard.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Carius sealed-tube oxidation to weighable AgX.
  • Ag/X mass ratios convert precipitate to halogen.
Remember
  • Sealed tubes pressure-digest halogens completely.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Carius method estimates halogens as precipitate of

Solution: Weighed AgX converts via atomic-mass ratios.
Example 1.

Q. 0.40 g of a bromo compound gave 0.47 g AgBr in Carius estimation. Find %Br. (Ag=108, Br=80)

  1. M(AgBr) = 188; Br fraction = 80/188.
  2. Br mass = 80/188 × 0.47 = 0.20 g; %Br = 0.20/0.40 × 100 = 50%.
  3. Sealed-tube fuming HNO3 ensures complete oxidation before precipitation.

Answer: %Br = 50% via AgBr gravimetry (80/188 ratio).

Chapter 1 · Topic 18

Estimation of sulphur

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Sulphur estimation (Carius: fuming HNO3 oxidises S to H2SO4, precipitated as BaSO4 with BaCl2 weighed - 32/233 ratio gives S) parallels halogen method with barium instead of silver. Complete oxidation (no SO2 escape) plus quantitative precipitation decide accuracy. Percentage S = 32/233 × (BaSO4/sample) × 100. Sulphur drugs and vulcanised rubber analysed this way routinely.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Carius oxidation to sulphate, BaSO4 weighed; 32/233 ratio.
  • No SO2 escape plus full precipitation ensure accuracy.
Remember
  • Barium sulphate gravimetry measures sulphur.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Sulphur estimation by Carius weighs precipitate of

Solution: Barium sulphate mass converts via 32/233 sulphur ratio.
Example 1.

Q. 0.50 g of a sulphur compound gave 0.70 g BaSO4 (Carius). Find %S. (Ba=137, S=32)

  1. M(BaSO4) = 233; S fraction = 32/233.
  2. S mass = 32/233 × 0.70 = 0.096 g; %S = 0.096/0.50 × 100 = 19.2%.
  3. Fuming HNO3 must fully oxidise S to sulphate with no SO2 escape.

Answer: %S = 19.2% via BaSO4 gravimetry (32/233 ratio).

Chapter 1 · Topic 19

Estimation of phosphorus

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phosphorus estimation (sodium-peroxide fusion or HNO3 oxidation to phosphate, precipitated as ammonium phosphomolybdate weighed, or Mg2P2O7 via magnesia mixture) quantifies P gravimetrically. Fusion must fully oxidise organic phosphorus (incomplete fusion under-reads); precipitate composition fixed by formula ratios. Fertilisers (phosphate content) and biomolecules analysed identically - P2O5 equivalents report fertiliser grades.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Fusion to phosphate, molybdate precipitate weighed.
  • Complete oxidation decides accuracy.
Remember
  • Fertiliser P2O5 grades derive from phosphate analysis.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Phosphorus is estimated gravimetrically as precipitate of

Solution: Yellow molybdate mass converts to phosphorus content.
Example 1.

Q. A phosphate fertiliser sample is analysed by molybdate gravimetry. 1.00 g sample gave 0.50 g ammonium phosphomolybdate precipitate (molar mass 1876, contains 1 P per mole). Find %P. (P=31)

  1. Moles precipitate = 0.50/1876 = 2.665×10^-4 = moles P.
  2. P mass = 2.665×10^-4 × 31 = 0.00826 g; %P = 0.83%.
  3. Fertiliser grades report P2O5 equivalents converted from %P.

Answer: %P = 0.83% (one P per precipitate mole).

Chapter 1 · Topic 20

Calculation of empirical formula

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Empirical formula (simplest whole-number atom ratio from percentage composition: divide each percent by atomic mass, divide all by smallest, round to integers - multiply to clear fractions like 1.5×2) represents Erlenmeyer? no - represents ratio truth (CH2O for glucose, acetylene and benzene share CH). Multiple compounds share empirical formulas (isomers differ structurally); molecular formula needs molar mass multiple. Percentage-to-ratio arithmetic is exam staple.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Percent to moles (÷atomic mass), divide by smallest, integerise.
  • Same empirical formula can hide different molecules.
Empirical steps
PointDetail
Step 1Percent ÷ atomic mass = moles
Step 2Divide all by smallest
Step 3Multiply to whole numbers
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Compound with 92.3% C, 7.7% H has empirical formula

Solution: Equal moles ratio 1:1 gives CH (benzene/acetylene share it).
Example 1.

Q. A compound has 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. Find its empirical formula.

  1. Moles: C = 40/12 = 3.33, H = 6.7/1 = 6.7, O = 53.3/16 = 3.33.
  2. Divide by smallest (3.33): C:H:O = 1:2:1.
  3. Empirical formula CH2O (could be glucose, formaldehyde or acetic acid sharing it).

Answer: CH2O - ratio 1:2:1 from mole division.

Example 2.

Q. A hydrocarbon has 92.3% C and 7.7% H. Find its empirical formula.

  1. Moles: C = 92.3/12 = 7.69, H = 7.7/1 = 7.7.
  2. Ratio 7.69:7.7 ≈ 1:1.
  3. Empirical formula CH (benzene C6H6 and acetylene C2H2 share it).

Answer: CH - equal moles give 1:1 ratio.

Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 1 · Topic 21

Calculation of molecular formula

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Molecular formula (actual atom counts = empirical × n, where n = molar mass ÷ empirical mass) needs colligative/colligative? no - molar mass via Victor Meyer, freezing-point depression, or mass spectrometry (molecular-ion peak). Glucose (CH2O × 6 = C6H12O6, n=6 from 180/30); benzene (CH × 6). Same empirical, different molecular formulas distinguished only by molar mass - analysis pairs both methods always.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Empirical multiple n = molar mass ÷ empirical mass.
  • Mass spectrometry reads molecular mass directly.
Remember
  • Empirical gives ratio; molar mass gives multiple.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Empirical CH with molar mass 78 has molecular formula

Solution: Multiple six expands CH to benzene C6H6.
Example 1.

Q. Empirical formula CH2O with molar mass 180 g/mol. Find molecular formula.

  1. Empirical mass = 12+2+16 = 30.
  2. n = 180/30 = 6; molecular = C6H12O6 (glucose).
  3. Molar mass from mass spectrometry (molecular-ion peak) or colligative methods.

Answer: C6H12O6 (n=6).

Example 2.

Q. Empirical CH (mass 13) with vapour density 39. Find molecular formula.

  1. Molar mass = 2 × VD = 78.
  2. n = 78/13 = 6; molecular = C6H6 (benzene).
  3. Vapour density doubles to molar mass for gases.

Answer: C6H6 (n=6 from M=78).

Chapter 1 · Topic 22

Organic quantitative analysis

Purification and Characterisation of Organic CompoundsPurification and GOCQuantitative AnalysisStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Quantitative analysis workflow: purify sample (impurities wreck percentages), estimate elements (combustion, Kjeldahl/Dumas, Carius gravimetry), compute empirical formula (mole ratios), measure molar mass (Victor Meyer, cryoscopy, mass spec), multiply to molecular formula - then confirm by synthesis or spectra. Each stage guards the next (impure samples mislead all downstream maths). Classical gravimetry plus modern spectroscopy together certify structures.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Purify, estimate, ratio-empirical, mass-molecular, confirm.
  • Impure samples corrupt every downstream number.
Remember
  • Analysis order: pure sample first, maths second.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

First step before any quantitative estimation must be

Solution: Impurities distort every percentage measured downstream.
Example 1.

Q. Plan the full analysis of an unknown containing C, H, N and Br.

  1. Purify first (melting-point constancy), then Lassaigne qualitative (N blue, Br silver precipitate).
  2. Quantify: Liebig combustion (C, H), Kjeldahl (N - valid, no nitro group), Carius AgBr (Br).
  3. Compute empirical formula, measure molar mass, multiply to molecular formula.

Answer: Purify → identify (Lassaigne) → quantify (combustion/Kjeldahl/Carius) → formulae.

Deep Dive · Structure decides reactivity

Electronic effects (inductive, mesomeric, hyperconjugation) plus stability orders plus priority rules answer most GOC questions.
NEET facts:
  • Carbocation 3° > 2° > 1°; same order for radicals; resonance beats hyperconjugation.
  • Acids outrank all listed groups for IUPAC suffix rights.

Most stable among given carbocations (methyl, ethyl, isopropyl, tert-butyl) is

Chapter 2 · Topic 1

Basic concepts

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Basic organic concepts: carbon tetravalency (four bonds, tetrahedral 109.5°) enables chains, branches, rings and networks no other element matches; catenation (C-C bonds rivalling C-X strengths) builds skeletons; isomerism (same formula, different structures) multiplies diversity; functional groups (reactive centres) classify reactivity; homologous series (CH2-graded families) predict trends. Tetravalency plus catenation plus isomerism explain organic millions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Tetravalent carbon catenates into chains-rings-networks.
  • Functional groups classify; homologous series predict trends.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Carbon shows tetravalency with geometry usually

Solution: Four single bonds point to tetrahedron corners.

Explanation

Concept. Electromeric effect (GOC (General Organic Chemistry), topic 3/34) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
Compare resonance $>$ hyperconjugation $>$ $+I$; $-I$ falls with distance
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Electromeric effect” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Explanation

Key formula / trend to memorise
$HA\\rightleftharpoons H^++A^-$; $ClCH_2COOH>HCOOH>CH_3COOH$; phenol $pK_a\\approx10$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Acids and bases in organic chemistry” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Explanation

Concept. Strength of organic acids (GOC (General Organic Chemistry), topic 14/34) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$HA\\rightleftharpoons H^++A^-$; $ClCH_2COOH>HCOOH>CH_3COOH$; phenol $pK_a\\approx10$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).

Chapter 2 · Topic 2

Tetravalency of carbon

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Tetravalency (carbon forming four covalent bonds: single-double-triple combinations totalling four) arises from four valence electrons (2s2 2p2) promoting-hybridising to bond fully - methane CH4 archetype. Silicon shares group but weak Si-Si bonds limit catenation (no silicon biochemistry); lead tetravalency poisons (tetraethyl lead). Four-bond capacity plus strength makes carbon uniquely prolific.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Four bonds per carbon from 2s2 2p2 promotion-hybridisation.
  • Silicon parallels group but cannot catenate strongly.
Remember
  • Four bonds always total (singles count one, triples three).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Methane carbon forms bonds numbering

Solution: Tetravalent carbon saturates with four hydrogens.
Example 1.

Q. Carbon forms 4 bonds while silicon (same group) rarely catenates. Explain with bond strengths.

  1. Tetravalency needs 4 strong bonds; C-C (~347 kJ/mol) rivals C-H/C-O strengths, so chains survive.
  2. Si-Si (~226 kJ/mol) is far weaker than Si-O (~452 kJ/mol) - chains oxidise apart instead of persisting.
  3. Strong catenation needs self-bonds rivalling hetero-bonds; only carbon qualifies.

Answer: C-C strength sustains chains; weak Si-Si collapses to silicates.

Chapter 2 · Topic 3

Shapes of simple molecules

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Molecular shapes follow VSEPR (electron pairs repel: linear CO2/BeCl2 180°, trigonal BF3 120°, tetrahedral CH4 109.5°, pyramidal NH3, bent H2O) with hybridisation matching geometry (sp linear, sp2 trigonal, sp3 tetrahedral). Lone pairs compress angles (ammonia 107°, water 104.5°). Shape decides polarity, reactivity and spectra - geometry underlies all organic stereochemistry.
NEET Snapshot:
  • VSEPR repulsions set shapes; hybridisation matches them.
  • Lone pairs squeeze angles below ideal.
Shape map
PointDetail
Linear 180°CO2, sp
Trigonal 120°BF3, sp2
Tetrahedral 109.5°CH4, sp3
Pyramidal/bentNH3/H2O, lone pairs
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Ammonia shape is pyramidal (not tetrahedral) because of

Solution: Lone-pair repulsion compresses H-N-H below 109.5°.
Example 1.

Q. Predict shapes: CO2, BF3, CH4, NH3, H2O using VSEPR.

  1. CO2: 2 bond pairs, 0 lone pairs - linear 180°.
  2. BF3: 3 bond pairs - trigonal planar 120°.
  3. CH4: 4 bond pairs - tetrahedral 109.5°; NH3: 3+1 lone pair - pyramidal ~107°; H2O: 2+2 lone pairs - bent ~104.5°.
  4. Lone pairs compress angles in NH3 and H2O below tetrahedral.

Answer: CO2 linear, BF3 trigonal, CH4 tetrahedral, NH3 pyramidal, H2O bent.

  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Homocyclic and heterocyclic compounds” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 2 · Topic 6

Functional groups

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Functional groups (reactive atom clusters: -OH alcohols, -CHO aldehydes, >C=O ketones, -COOH acids, -NH2 amines, -X halides, -OR ethers, C=C alkenes, C≡C alkynes) decide reaction families - same group reacts similarly across molecules. Priority order (acids > anhydrides > esters > halides > amides > nitriles > aldehydes > ketones > alcohols > amines) names principal groups as suffixes, others as prefixes. Recognising groups predicts reactions instantly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Reactive clusters classifying reaction families.
  • Priority decides suffix (principal) versus prefix.
Remember
  • Learn priorities cold - nomenclature depends on order.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Highest nomenclature priority among these belongs to

Solution: Acids outrank all listed groups as suffix choosers.
Example 1.

Q. An unknown (mol. formula C3H6O) gives orange DNP precipitate but no silver mirror. Identify the class.

  1. DNP orange proves carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone).
  2. No Tollens mirror rules out aldehydes (no oxidisable H).
  3. Must be a ketone (acetone/propanone) - carbonyl without aldehydic H.

Answer: Ketone (propanone) - DNP-positive, Tollens-negative.

Back to Index
Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 2 · Topic 7

Organic compounds containing halogens

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Halogen-containing organics (alkyl halides R-X, aryl halides Ar-X, vinyl/allyl/benzylic variants) centre C-X polarity (Cδ+-Xδ- from electronegativity) driving substitution-elimination chemistry. Reactivity (R-I > R-Br > R-Cl >> R-F bond-strength order) plus type (allyl/benzyl 1° > 2° > 1° alkyl for SN1; reverse for SN2) patterns fill chapters. DDT, chloroform, freons show halogen chemistry scaling to environment.
NEET Snapshot:
  • C-X polarity drives substitution-elimination reactivity.
  • I > Br > Cl >> F reactivity follows bond weakness.
Remember
  • Allyl/benzyl halides ionise easiest (resonance cations).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most reactive alkyl halide toward substitution is the

Solution: Weak C-I bonds break fastest in rate steps.
Example 1.

Q. Arrange: CH3F, CH3Cl, CH3Br, CH3I in order of C-X bond strength and SN reactivity.

  1. Bond strength: C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I (shorter binds tighter).
  2. SN reactivity reverses: R-I > R-Br > R-Cl >> R-F (weaker breaks faster).
  3. Iodide is the best leaving group among halides.

Answer: Strength F>Cl>Br>I; reactivity I>Br>Cl>>F.

Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 2 · Topic 8

Organic compounds containing oxygen

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Oxygen organics (alcohols R-OH, phenols Ar-OH, ethers R-O-R, aldehydes R-CHO, ketones R2C=O, acids R-COOH, esters, anhydrides, amides) share carbonyl/hydroxyl chemistry with acidity-basicity gradients (acids > phenols > water > alcohols) and nucleophilic-addition (carbonyl) versus substitution (acyl) pathways. Oxidation ladders (alcohol-aldehyde-acid) plus reduction reverses interconvert classes - oxygen content tracks oxidation state.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hydroxyl/carbonyl families with acidity and addition chemistry.
  • Oxidation ladders interconvert alcohol-aldehyde-acid.
Remember
  • Acids > phenols > water > alcohols acidity order.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most acidic among alcohol, phenol, water and acid is

Solution: Resonance-stabilised carboxylate makes acids strongest.
Example 1.

Q. Ethanol (bp 78°C) vs dimethyl ether (bp -24°C), same formula C2H6O. Explain.

  1. Ethanol H-bonds (O-H donors) forming associated liquids - high boiling.
  2. Dimethyl ether cannot H-bond donate (no O-H); only weak dipole forces - gas at room temperature.
  3. Functional group decides intermolecular forces, hence boiling points.

Answer: H-bonding ethanol boils high; non-H-bonding ether stays gaseous.

Back to Index
Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 2 · Topic 9

Organic compounds containing nitrogen

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nitrogen organics (amines R-NH2, nitro R-NO2, nitriles R-CN, amides R-CONH2, diazonium Ar-N2+, amino acids) span base (amines), explosive (nitro), solvent (amides/DMF), dye (diazonium coupling) and life (amino acids) roles. Basicity (alkyl pushes up, aryl delocalises down, aqueous solvation reshuffles gas-phase orders) plus diazotisation (cold NaNO2/HCl) dominate reactions. Nitrogen versatility rivals oxygen in organic importance.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Amines basic, nitro explosive, nitriles versatile, diazonium dyes.
  • Aqueous basicity reshuffles gas-phase orders (solvation).
Remember
  • Aniline < ammonia < alkylamines (aqueous) typical order.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most basic in aqueous solution among given is usually

Solution: Alkyl donation plus solvation favour aliphatic amines.
Example 1.

Q. Ethanamine (bp 17°C) vs ethylenediamine (bp 117°C). Why such a gap?

  1. Ethanamine: one -NH2, moderate H-bonding.
  2. Ethylenediamine: two -NH2 groups doubling H-bond donors/acceptors - far stronger association.
  3. More H-bonding sites raise boiling dramatically.

Answer: Two amino groups double hydrogen bonding vs one.

Back to Index
Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 2 · Topic 10

Organic compounds containing sulphur

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Sulphur organics (thiols R-SH, sulphides R-S-R, disulphides, sulphonic acids R-SO3H detergents, mustard-gas historical) mirror oxygen chemistry with bigger, softer atoms (stronger nucleophiles, weaker H-bonds, smelly volatiles). Disulphide bridges lock protein shapes (hair permanent waves break-reform them); thiol-ene click chemistry builds polymers. Garlic allicin plus skunk thiols show sulphur smell signatures.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Oxygen analogues with softer, smellier, stronger-nucleophile character.
  • Disulphides lock protein tertiary shapes.
Remember
  • Permanent waves break and reform disulphide bridges.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Disulphide bridges stabilise protein structure via amino acid

Solution: Cysteine thiols oxidise into covalent S-S links.
Example 1.

Q. Garlic smell (allicin) and skunk spray (thiols) share which element? What protein feature uses it?

  1. Both are organosulphur compounds - pungent volatile sulphur signatures.
  2. Cysteine disulphide (S-S) bridges lock protein tertiary shapes; permanent waves break and reform them.
  3. Sulphur smell plus disulphide structure roles.

Answer: Sulphur - smelly volatiles outside, disulphide bridges inside proteins.

Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 2 · Topic 11

Homologous series

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBasicsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Homologous series (same functional group, CH2-graded neighbours: alkanes methane-ethane-propane, alcohols methanol-ethanol, acids formic-acetic) show graded physical trends (boiling points rise ~20-30°C per CH2) with near-identical chemistry (same group reacts alike). Prediction power (unknown member properties interpolate) plus nomenclature regularity (one suffix per series) organise millions into families. Methylene-difference neighbours behave as chemical siblings.
NEET Snapshot:
  • CH2-stepped families with graded physics, similar chemistry.
  • Boiling points rise steadily per added CH2.
Remember
  • Same group, same reactions - series predict behaviour.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Homologous series differ between neighbours by group

Solution: Methylene increments grade physical properties smoothly.
Example 1.

Q. First three alkanes: methane (gas), ethane (gas), propane (gas), butane (gas), pentane (liquid). Explain the trend break.

  1. Boiling rises ~20-30°C per CH2 (surface area grows).
  2. Pentane crosses room temperature first - C1-C4 gases, C5+ liquids.
  3. Homologous gradation predicts physical states.

Answer: Boiling climbs per CH2; pentane first liquid at room temperature.

Counting strategies (symmetry reduction, longest-chain systematics) plus the detailed type sections attached here drill every variant.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Same atoms, different bonds - connectivity isomerism.
  • DBE constrains rings-plus-pi-bonds count.
Remember
  • DBE = C - H/2 + N/2 + 1 guides all counting.

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Explanation

Concept. Counting structural isomers (Structural Isomerism, topic 8/16) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$IHD=(2C+2+N-H-X)/2$; $C_4H_{10}O$=7 (4 alcohols+3 ethers)
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Counting structural isomers” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Stereoisomerism

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCIsomerismStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Stereoisomerism (same connectivity, different spatial arrangement: geometrical cis-trans across double bonds/rings, optical isomerism from chirality) needs 3D vision - wedge-dash, Fischer, Newman and sawhorse projections translate. Cis-trans (Cahn-Ingold priorities E/Z), R/S chirality, meso versus racemic distinctions fill chapters. Old o2 chapter (stereoisomerism masterclass) covers this unit deeply - refer its sections for full drill.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Geometrical (cis-trans/E-Z) plus optical (R/S, meso, racemic).
  • Same bonds, different space - 3D projections decode.
Remember
  • E/Z by priorities; R/S by chiral centres; meso cancels internally.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Geometrical isomerism requires

Solution: Locked rotation plus distinct substituents enable cis-trans pairs.
Example 1.

Q. How many stereoisomers does 2-butene show? Draw and label them.

  1. Restricted C=C rotation with two different groups per carbon (CH3/H each side) allows cis-trans.
  2. cis-But-2-ene (both CH3 same side, polar) and trans-but-2-ene (opposite, non-polar).
  3. No chiral centres, so no optical isomers - two geometrical isomers only.

Answer: Two: cis- and trans-but-2-ene.

Chapter 2 · Topic 15

Nomenclature

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCNomenclatureStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. IUPAC system basics (Nomenclature, topic 1/22) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$HA\\rightleftharpoons H^++A^-$; $ClCH_2COOH>HCOOH>CH_3COOH$; phenol $pK_a\\approx10$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “IUPAC system basics” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 2 · Topic 16

Trivial nomenclature

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCNomenclatureStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Trivial (common) names (acetic acid, acetone, toluene, glycerine, formalin) persist from history/discovery - short, memorable, still legal in trade and some exams, but unsystematic (no structure decoding). Formic (ants), acetic (vinegar), butyric (butter) acids name sources; acetone, acetophenone trade names dominate industry. IUPAC preferred names standardise science; trivial names survive commerce - know both, write IUPAC in answers.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Historical short names (acetic acid, toluene) persist commercially.
  • Unsystematic but entrenched - learn alongside IUPAC.
Remember
  • Formic ants, acetic vinegar - source-named acids.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Acetone is the trivial name of

Solution: Simplest ketone trades as acetone universally.
Example 1.

Q. Convert trivial names to structures: acetone, toluene, glycerine.

  1. Acetone = propan-2-one (simplest ketone).
  2. Toluene = methylbenzene.
  3. Glycerine = propane-1,2,3-triol (glycerol).
  4. Trivial names memorised; IUPAC derived systematically.

Answer: Propan-2-one, methylbenzene, propane-1,2,3-triol.

Chapter 2 · Topic 17

IUPAC nomenclature

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCNomenclatureStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

IUPAC nomenclature systematises: longest principal chain, principal functional group suffix (priority order), numbering lowest locants, alphabetical prefixes (di/tri multipliers ignored), stereochemistry (E/Z, R/S) tagged. Suffixes (-oic acid, -al, -one, -ol, -amine) plus prefixes (halo, nitro, alkoxy) encode structures reversibly - names draw structures, structures name back. Priority order (acids top, amines bottom among listed) decides suffix choice always.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Longest chain, principal suffix, lowest numbers, alphabetical prefixes.
  • Priority order picks suffix; rest become prefixes.
Priority (high to low)
PointDetail
Acids-oic acid suffix
Aldehydes/ketones-al/-one
Alcohols/amines-ol/-amine
Halo/nitro/alkoxyprefixes only
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Principal group -COOH versus -OH names the compound as

Solution: Acid outranks alcohol for suffix rights.
Example 1.

Q. Name CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CHO by IUPAC rules.

  1. Longest chain including -CHO: 3 carbons (propanal root, aldehyde C-1).
  2. Methyl substituent at C-2.
  3. 2-Methylpropanal.

Answer: 2-Methylpropanal (aldehyde carbon always C-1).

Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 2 · Topic 18

Bond fission

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBond Fission and IntermediatesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Bond fission splits covalent bonds: homolytic (equal electron sharing - one electron each, free radicals, heat/light/peroxides trigger) versus heterolytic (unequal - both electrons to more electronegative partner, ions in polar solvents). Fission mode decides intermediate (radicals vs ions) and thus reaction family (substitution patterns, rearrangements). Curved full arrows track ion pairs; fish-hooks track single electrons - notation matches mechanism.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Homolytic shares equally (radicals); heterolytic gifts both (ions).
  • Full arrows for ions, fish-hooks for radicals.
Remember
  • Polar solvents favour heterolysis; heat/light favour homolysis.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Homolytic fission produces

Solution: Equal electron splitting makes radical pairs.
Example 1.

Q. Cl2/UV versus aqueous KOH on ethane: which fission mode operates in each?

  1. Cl2/UV: heat-light homolysis - Cl· radicals start chains (homolytic).
  2. Aqueous KOH ionises (heterolytic conditions), but ethane C-H bonds resist both - no reaction either way.
  3. Fission mode follows conditions: light/heat radical, polar media ionic.

Answer: Cl2/UV homolytic (no reaction with ethane anyway); KOH heterolytic conditions.

Index / Purification and GOC
Chapter 2 · Topic 19

Homolytic fission

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBond Fission and IntermediatesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Homolytic and heterolytic bond cleavage (GOC (General Organic Chemistry), topic 25/34) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$sp^3$ $109.5^\\circ$, $sp^2$ $120^\\circ$, $sp$ $180^\\circ$; $DBE=C-H/2+N/2+1$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Homolytic and heterolytic bond cleavage” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 2 · Topic 20

Heterolytic fission

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBond Fission and IntermediatesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Heterolytic fission (both bonding electrons to more electronegative atom: C-X to C+ plus X-, C-H to C- plus H+ reversely) makes ion pairs needing polar-solvent stabilisation - SN1/E1 ionisations, acid-base events. Electronegativity gaps drive direction (halogens take pairs from carbon; metals lose to carbon in Grignards). Solvolysis rates track ion stability (3° fastest) plus solvent polarity - fission feasibility decides mechanisms.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Both electrons to electronegative partner forming ions.
  • Polar solvents stabilise ion pairs enabling heterolysis.
Remember
  • SN1 ionises heterolytically; peroxides homolyse instead.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Carbocations form by heterolytic fission of bond

Solution: Electronegative halogens capture bonding pairs leaving cations.
Example 1.

Q. tert-Butyl chloride hydrolyses instantly in aqueous acetone; methyl chloride needs heating. Explain via fission.

  1. tert-Butyl chloride heterolyses to stable 3° carbocation (fast SN1).
  2. Methyl chloride cannot ionise (methyl cation unstable) - needs SN2 heating.
  3. Heterolysis rate follows carbocation stability ladder.

Answer: Stable-cation substrates ionise fast; unstable ones need SN2 push.

Chapter 2 · Topic 25

Nucleophiles

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBond Fission and IntermediatesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Nucleophiles (electron-rich donors: neutral amines, alcohols, water; anionic OH-, CN-, RO-; pi-bonds) attack electron-poor centres (carbocations, carbonyl carbons, alkyl halide carbons) donating pairs - strength tracks polarisability and charge (I- > Br- > Cl- > F- in protic solvents; reverse in aprotic). Ambident nucleophiles (CN-, enolates) attack through alternative atoms giving product mixtures. Donor strength plus solvent decide rates.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Electron donors attacking positive centres.
  • Polarisable anions dominate protic solvents.
Nucleophile ladder (protic)
PointDetail
StrongestI-, HS-, RS- (polarisable)
MediumBr-, OH-, CN-
WeakestF-, H2O, ROH
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Strongest nucleophile in protic solvents among halides is

Solution: Large diffuse iodide donates easiest when solvated.
Example 1.

Q. Arrange CN-, F-, I-, H2O as nucleophiles in protic solvents with reason.

  1. I- > CN- > F- > H2O in protic media (polarisability beats basicity; solvation tames small F-).
  2. Large diffuse iodide donates easiest when hydrogen-bonded.
  3. In aprotic solvents the order reverses toward basicity (F- strongest).

Answer: I- > CN- > F- > H2O (protic); solvent flips the ladder.

Chapter 2 · Topic 26

Stability of carbocations

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBond Fission and IntermediatesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Carbocation stability (3° > 2° > 1° > methyl via hyperconjugation plus inductive donation; resonance (allyl, benzyl) beats alkyl; electron-withdrawing neighbours destabilise) decides SN1 rates, rearrangements (hydride/methyl shifts to stabler cations) and elimination regiochemistry (Saytzeff most-substituted alkenes). Non-classical (bridged) and vinyl/aryl (unstable, avoid) extremes frame the scale. Stability predicts pathways - reactions route through lowest-energy cations.
NEET Snapshot:
  • 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl; resonance beats hyperconjugation.
  • Rearrangements climb stability ladders (H-/Me- shifts).
Remember
  • Benzyl/allyl resonance outranks tert-butyl hyperconjugation.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most stable carbocation among methyl, ethyl, isopropyl, tert-butyl is

Solution: Nine hyperconjugative hydrogens stabilise tert-butyl best.

Explanation

Concept. Carbocation rearrangements (GOC (General Organic Chemistry), topic 30/34) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$R_3C^+$, order $3^\\circ>2^\\circ>1^\\circ$; $CH_3CH_2CH_2^+\\to CH_3CH^+CH_3$ by 1,2-H shift
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Carbocation rearrangements” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 2 · Topic 27

Stability of free radicals

Some Basic Principles of Organic ChemistryPurification and GOCBond Fission and IntermediatesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Free-radical stability (3° > 2° > 1°, resonance allyl/benzyl best via delocalisation, hyperconjugation assists) mirrors cations (no charge solvation effects) - bond dissociation energies quantify (allylic C-H weakest). Stability decides halogenation selectivity (tertiary H abstracted fastest: 3° > 2° > 1° = 5:3.5:1 rates), polymerisation initiation and antioxidant action (vitamin E donates H making stable radicals). Parallel yet distinct from cation scales.
NEET Snapshot:
  • 3° > 2° > 1°; resonance delocalisation dominates.
  • Halogenation selectivity follows radical stability.
Remember
  • Tertiary hydrogens abstract fastest in bromination.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Deep Dive · Skeletons with personalities

Hydrocarbons run alkanes (structure, classification, nomenclature with haloalkane extras, Wurtz-Kolbe-decarboxylation preparations, properties, reactions with cracking extras, conformations with Newman-stability extras, radical halogenation with Finkelstein? no - with free-radical extras) through alkenes (structure to polymerisation with Markovnikov-hydroboration-ozonolysis extras) and alkynes (structure to addition with acidic-acetylide extras) into aromatics (benzene structure, Huckel aromaticity, electrophilic substitution with directing-group extras, Friedel-Crafts with limitations). Saturation decides mechanism: substitute alkanes, add to alkenes, preserve aromatic rings.
NEET facts:
  • Markovnikov via stabler cations (peroxide-HBr exception); Saytzeff most-substituted alkenes.
  • Huckel 4n+2 pi electrons defines aromaticity; Lindlar gives cis, Na/NH3 trans.
Fig: Substitute alkanes, add to alkenes twice to alkynes, preserve aromatic rings.

Chapter 3 · Topic 2

Isomerism

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsA. GeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Hydrocarbon isomerism spans skeletons (chain branching: n-butane vs isobutane), positions (double-bond location: but-1-ene vs but-2-ene), functional classes (alkene vs cycloalkane sharing CnH2n), conformations (staggered-eclipsed rotations, chair-boat cyclohexane), and geometrical cis-trans pairs. DBE (C - H/2 + N/2 + 1) constrains possibilities before drawing. More branching lowers boiling points (surface area shrinks) - property prediction from structure.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Chain, position, functional, conformational, geometrical - five isomer types.
  • Branching lowers boiling points; DBE guides counting.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

n-Butane and isobutane show isomerism of type

Solution: Same formula, different carbon skeletons - chain isomerism.
Example 1.

Q. C4H8 shows three structural types. Identify them.

  1. But-1-ene/but-2-ene (alkenes, position isomers).
  2. Methylpropene (branched alkene).
  3. Cyclobutane/methylcyclopropane (ring isomers, same formula).
  4. Chain, position and ring-chain isomerism in one formula.

Answer: Alkenes (straight/branched) plus cycloalkanes - same atoms, rebuilt skeletons.

Chapter 3 · Topic 3

IUPAC nomenclature

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsA. GeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Hydrocarbon IUPAC names build systematically: longest carbon chain as parent (alkane/alkene/alkyne suffix by saturation), lowest locants for multiple bonds and branches, alphabetical substituents (di/tri multipliers ignored), cyclo- prefix for rings, benzene for aromatics. Common names (ethylene, acetylene, toluene) persist commercially. Name-to-structure reversibility (draw from name, name from drawing) is the examined skill both directions.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical branches.
  • Ethylene (ethene), acetylene (ethyne) trivial survivors.
Remember
  • Number to give multiple bonds lowest locants first.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

IUPAC name of acetylene is

Solution: Two-carbon triple bond names ethyne systematically.
Example 1.

Q. Name (CH3)2CH-CH2-C triple CH by IUPAC rules.

  1. Longest chain including triple bond: 4 carbons (butyne).
  2. Triple bond gets lowest locant: but-1-yne; methyl at C-3.
  3. 3-Methylbut-1-yne.

Answer: 3-Methylbut-1-yne (triple bond priority in numbering).

Chapter 3 · Topic 4

Methods of preparation

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsA. GeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Hydrocarbon preparation toolbox: hydrogenation (unsaturates to alkanes, Ni/Pt/Pd), Wurtz coupling (alkyl halides plus Na to longer alkanes), Kolbe electrolysis (decarboxylative coupling), decarboxylation (soda-lime to alkanes), dehydration (alcohols to alkenes, Saytzeff major), dehydrohalogenation (alkyl halides plus alcoholic KOH), calcium carbide plus water (acetylene), cracking (heavy to light fractions). Method choice follows target skeleton plus available feedstock.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hydrogenate, couple (Wurtz/Kolbe), dehydrate, crack, carbide-to-acetylene.
  • Dehydration follows Saytzeff (more substituted alkene).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Acetylene is prepared in the laboratory from calcium carbide plus

Solution: CaC2 hydrolysis releases acetylene gas.
Example 1.

Q. Prepare propene from isopropanol and from 1-bromopropane.

  1. Isopropanol with conc. H2SO4 (heat): dehydration, Saytzeff propene.
  2. 1-Bromopropane with alcoholic KOH: dehydrohalogenation to propene.
  3. Acid dehydrates alcohols; alcoholic base eliminates HX.

Answer: Dehydration (acid) and dehydrohalogenation (alcoholic KOH).

Chapter 3 · Topic 5

Properties

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsA. GeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Hydrocarbon properties follow structure: boiling points rise with mass, fall with branching (surface contact rules); alkanes inert (paraffins - affinity-less, needing heat/light to react); alkenes-alkynes add readily (pi bonds break easily); aromatics substitute preserving rings. Density below water (float), insolubility in water (oil spills spread), solubility in organics - physical constants identify unknowns practically.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Boiling rises with mass, falls with branching.
  • Alkanes inert, alkenes add, aromatics substitute - reactivity ladder.
Remember
  • Paraffin means affinity-less - alkane inertness named.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Boiling point order among pentane isomers is highest for

Solution: Straight chains contact most, attracting strongest.
Example 1.

Q. Ethene (gas) vs decene (liquid): explain using homologous trends.

  1. Boiling rises ~20-30C per CH2 (surface area grows).
  2. C2 ethene boils at -104C; C10 decene near 170C.
  3. Homologous gradation predicts physical states.

Answer: Mass-driven boiling climb across the alkene series.

Back to Index
Index / Hydrocarbons and Halogen Compounds
Chapter 3 · Topic 6

Reactions

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsA. GeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Hydrocarbon reactions split by bond type: alkanes substitute via free radicals (halogenation, nitration, sulphonation under harsh conditions), alkenes-alkynes add electrophilically (Markovnikov, peroxides, ozonolysis cleavage), aromatics substitute electrophilically (ring preserved via arenium ions), all combust to CO2 plus water (calorific values rank fuels). Oxidation (KMnO4, ozone) cleaves or hydroxylates diagnostically - Baeyer test decolourises for unsaturation.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Substitute (alkanes), add (alkenes), substitute preserving ring (aromatics).
  • Combustion plus Baeyer unsaturation test complete the set.
Reaction families
PointDetail
AlkanesFree-radical substitution
Alkenes/alkynesElectrophilic addition
AromaticsElectrophilic substitution (ring kept)
AllCombustion to CO2 + H2O
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Baeyer test (cold KMnO4 decolourisation) detects

Solution: Pi bonds reduce purple permanganate to brown MnO2.
Example 1.

Q. Propene with HBr (no peroxide) vs with HBr/peroxide. Give products.

  1. No peroxide: Markovnikov - H to terminal carbon (stabler 2° cation), Br to middle: 2-bromopropane.
  2. Peroxide: anti-Markovnikov radical chain - Br to terminal carbon: 1-bromopropane.
  3. Ionic vs radical mechanisms flip orientation.

Answer: 2-Bromopropane (Markovnikov) vs 1-bromopropane (peroxide effect).

Chapter 3 · Topic 8

Classification

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsB. AlkanesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkanes classify by carbon connectivity: normal (straight chains), iso (one secondary branch, 2-methyl prefix), neo (tert-butyl ends, 2,2-dimethyl) - boiling points fall n > iso > neo (surface shrinking). Primary/secondary/tertiary/quaternary carbons (1/2/3/4 carbon neighbours) predict reactivity (3° H abstracts fastest) and naming. Cycloalkanes (rings: cyclopropane to cyclohexane, Baeyer strain in small rings) parallel open chains.
NEET Snapshot:
  • n/iso/neo by branching; 1°/2°/3°/4° carbons by neighbours.
  • Cycloalkanes ring the same chemistry with strain.
Remember
  • Tertiary hydrogens abstract fastest in halogenation.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Neopentane IUPAC name revealing its class is

Solution: Central carbon with four methyls is doubly branched neo-alkane.
Example 1.

Q. Classify: n-butane, isobutane, cyclobutane.

  1. n-Butane: normal straight-chain alkane.
  2. Isobutane (2-methylpropane): branched-chain alkane.
  3. Cyclobutane: cycloalkane (ring, angle-strained).
  4. Straight, branched and ring classes.

Answer: n-, iso- and cyclo-alkane classes.

Nomenclature

Topic in Depth

Alkane nomenclature: longest continuous chain as parent (meth through dec plus), methyl-ethyl-propyl substituents numbered lowest, alphabetical order (di/tri ignored), cyclo- prefix with ring numbering, common names (isobutane, neopentane) retained. Haloalkanes name halogen prefixes (fluoro/chloro/bromo/iodo) with locants. Drawing from names (skeleton first, substituents after) reverses the skill symmetrically.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Longest chain, lowest locants, alphabetical branches.
  • Haloalkanes prefix halogens with locants.
Remember
  • Alphabetise ignoring di/tri multipliers.

Key formula / trend to memorise
$C_6H_6+E^+\\to[C_6H_6E]^+\\to C_6H_5E$; $o,p$: $OH,NH_2,R,X$; $m$: $NO_2,CN,COR$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Kolbe electrolysis” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 3 · Topic 12

Reactions

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsB. AlkanesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkane reactions need harsh initiation (heat/light breaking C-H homolytically): free-radical halogenation (Cl2/UV, Br2 selective 3°>2°>1°), nitration (fuming HNO3, high T/P), sulphonation, oxidation/combustion (fuels), cracking (thermal/catalytic to smaller alkenes plus hydrogen), isomerisation (AlCl3 reshuffling), aromatisation (n-hexane to benzene, Pt reforming). Inertness is relative - energy input unlocks radical chains.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Halogenation, nitration, combustion, cracking, isomerisation, aromatisation.
  • Radical chains need heat/light initiation.
Remember
  • Bromination selectivity 1600:82:1 (3°:2°:1°) is extreme.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Halogenation of alkanes proceeds via mechanism that is

Solution: Heat/light homolysis starts radical substitution chains.
