Chapter 3 · Topic 15

Structure

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsC. AlkenesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkene structure (C=C double bond: one sigma plus one pi, 120° trigonal planar, restricted rotation) enables cis-trans isomerism and addition chemistry - pi electrons exposed above-below planes attract electrophiles. Bond length shortens (134 pm vs 154 pm single), strength rises (not doubles - pi weaker than sigma). Conjugated dienes (alternating double-single) delocalise specially (1,4-addition, Diels-Alder); isolated and cumulated variants differ.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sigma plus pi planar units with locked rotation.
  • Pi exposure drives addition; restriction enables cis-trans.
Remember
  • Cis-trans needs restricted rotation plus two different groups.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Restricted rotation about C=C enables isomerism called

Solution: Locked double bonds freeze substituent geometries.
Example 1.

Q. Ethyne is linear while ethene is planar. Explain via hybridisation.

  1. Ethyne carbons sp (180°) - triple bond linear geometry.
  2. Ethene carbons sp2 (120°) - double bond trigonal planar.
  3. Hybridisation sets geometry: sp linear, sp2 planar, sp3 tetrahedral.

Answer: sp linear (180°) vs sp2 planar (120°) geometries.

Back to Index
Index / Hydrocarbons and Halogen Compounds
Chapter 3 · Topic 16

Nomenclature

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsC. AlkenesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkene nomenclature numbers to give double bonds lowest locants (but-1-ene vs but-2-ene), -ene suffix replacing -ane, substituents alphabetical, E/Z (Cahn-Ingold priorities across bond) replacing simple cis-trans where needed, cycloalkenes numbered through double bonds. Common names (ethylene, propylene, styrene) persist industrially. Dienes/trienes count multiple bonds (buta-1,3-diene).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lowest locants for double bonds; E/Z by priorities.
  • Ethylene/propylene/styrene trivial survivors.
Remember
  • E/Z replaces cis-trans when priorities complicate.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

E/Z nomenclature is based on priority rules called

Solution: Atomic-number priorities rank substituents across bonds.
Example 1.

Q. Name CH triple C-CH2-CH3 by two systems.

  1. IUPAC: but-1-yne (4-carbon chain, triple bond C-1).
  2. Common: ethylacetylene (acetylene derivative).
  3. Systematic numbering beats trivial substitution names.

Answer: But-1-yne (IUPAC); ethylacetylene (common).

Chapter 3 · Topic 18

Properties

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsC. AlkenesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkene properties: gases to waxy solids by mass (boiling rises, branching lowers like alkanes), insoluble in water (pi hydrophobicity) soluble in organics, more stable with substitution (hyperconjugation: tetra > tri > di > mono - heat of hydrogenation proves), cis isomers polar (dipole moments) versus trans non-polar, weak dipole-dipole forces. Stability order predicts addition orientation (Markovnikov to stabler cations).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Substitution stabilises (hyperconjugation); cis polar, trans non-polar.
  • Heat of hydrogenation measures stability inversely.
Alkene stability

Tetra-substitutedMost stable
Tri-substitutedNext
Di/monoLess
Measured byHeat of hydrogenation (lower = stabler)

Chapter 3 · Topic 19

Reactions

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsC. AlkenesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkene reactions add across pi bonds: hydrogenation (Ni/Pt/Pd to alkanes), halogenation (Br2 test decolourises), hydrohalogenation (Markovnikov via stabler carbocations; peroxide anti-Markovnikov for HBr), hydration (acid to alcohols Markovnikov), hydroboration-oxidation (anti-Markovnikov alcohols), epoxidation (peracids), hydroxylation (cold KMnO4 syn diols - Baeyer test), ozonolysis (cleavage locating bonds). Electrophile attacks pi cloud first always.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hydrogenate, halogenate, hydrate, hydroxylate, cleave by ozone.
  • Markovnikov via stabler cations (peroxide exception for HBr).
Remember
  • Bromine water decolourising proves unsaturation instantly.

Chapter 3 · Topic 20

Geometrical isomerism

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsC. AlkenesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Geometrical isomerism (cis same-side, trans opposite-side across C=C or rings) needs restricted rotation plus two different groups per carbon - physical properties differ (cis polar higher boiling, trans packs better melting higher; maleic vs fumaric acids). E/Z extends to complex cases via Cahn-Ingold priorities. Aligned dipoles (cis) versus cancelled (trans) split boiling points; packing splits melting points oppositely.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cis (same side, polar) vs trans (opposite, packable).
  • E/Z generalises via priority rules.
Remember
  • Cis boils higher (polar); trans melts higher (packs).

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsC. AlkenesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Electrophilic addition (pi electrons attack electrophiles: protonation to stabler carbocation, nucleophile captures) runs Markovnikov orientation (H to less-substituted carbon making stabler cation; rearrangements possible), peroxide HBr exception (radical anti-Markovnikov), stereochemistry (bromonium anti-addition giving trans-dibromides; syn hydroxylation giving cis-diols). Carbocation stability dictates orientation; bridged ions dictate stereochemistry.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Protonate to stabler cation, capture nucleophile - orientation set.
  • Bromonium anti-addition; syn-hydroxylation - stereochemistry set.

MarkovnikovH to less-substituted (stabler cation)
Peroxide HBrAnti-Markovnikov (radical)
BromineAnti via bromonium bridge

Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Anti-Markovnikov addition” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Chapter 3 · Topic 24

Structure

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsD. AlkynesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkyne structure (C≡C triple bond: one sigma plus two pi, 180° linear, sp hybridised) enables acidity (terminal ≡C-H pKa ~25, deprotonated by strong bases to acetylides) and two-stage additions (alkene then alkane intermediates). Short strong bonds (120 pm); cylindrical pi clouds attack electrophiles twice. Terminal versus internal alkynes differ (acidic H present or not) - Tollens/Fehling-style ammoniacal precipitates diagnose terminal types.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Linear sp triple bonds; terminal H acidic (pKa ~25).
  • Two pi bonds add twice sequentially.
Remember
  • Acetylene acidity (terminal H) is alkyne-exclusive.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Terminal alkynes are acidic due to H attached to carbon that is

Solution: 50 percent s-character holds acetylide electrons close.
Example 1.

Q. Acetylene burns with ~3000C flame in oxyacetylene torches. Why so hot?

  1. Triple bond stores high energy (two pi bonds).
  2. Combustion C2H2 + 2.5O2 releases ~1300 kJ/mol concentrated in small flame.
  3. High energy density plus pure-oxygen burning peaks temperature.

Answer: Triple-bond energy plus oxygen-fed combustion concentrates heat.

Chapter 3 · Topic 25

Nomenclature

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsD. AlkynesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkyne nomenclature numbers triple bonds lowest (-yne suffix; -diyne/-triyne multiples), substituents alphabetical, common names (acetylene, methylacetylene/propyne) persist. Enyne compounds (double plus triple) number to give lowest set (double gets priority on ties). Disubstituted versus terminal classification (acidic H present or absent) matters more than names - reactivity follows substitution.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lowest locants for triple bonds; -yne suffix.
  • Acetylene/propyne trivial names survive industrially.
Remember
  • Double bonds win numbering ties over triples.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Common name methylacetylene is IUPAC

Solution: Three-carbon triple bond names propyne systematically.
Example 1.

Q. Name HC triple C-CH(CH3)2 by IUPAC rules.

  1. Longest chain with triple bond: 3 carbons (propyne root).
  2. Methyl at C-3? Numbering: triple bond gets locant 1: 3-methylbut-1-yne needs 4 carbons - recount: HC≡C-CH(CH3)2 has 4 carbons total.
  3. 3-Methylbut-1-yne.

Answer: 3-Methylbut-1-yne (longest 4-chain, triple bond C-1).

Chapter 3 · Topic 27

Properties

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsD. AlkynesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkyne properties: gases to solids by mass (lower boiling than corresponding alkenes/alkanes - weaker dispersion), insoluble water, weak polarity; terminal alkynes (acidic, metal-acetylide forming with Ag+/Cu+ ammoniacal - white/red precipitates diagnose), internal (non-acidic, no precipitates). Oxyacetylene flames (~3000°C) weld metals - combustion heat plus concentrated flame physics.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Lower boiling than alkene/alkane analogues.
  • Terminal acidity precipitates with Ag+/Cu+ ammoniacal.
Remember
  • Ammoniacal silver test diagnoses terminal alkynes.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Terminal alkynes give white precipitate with reagent

Solution: Acetylide silver salts precipitate diagnostically.
Example 1.

Q. Pent-1-yne vs pent-2-yne vs 2-methylbut-1-yne: how do properties differ?

  1. Boiling: straight pent-1-yne highest, branched methylbutyne lowest (surface area).
  2. Acidity: terminal (pent-1-yne, 2-methylbut-1-yne) acidic; internal (pent-2-yne) not.
  3. Ammoniacal AgNO3 precipitates only terminal pair.

Answer: Straight boils highest; terminal pair acidic, internal is not.

Chapter 3 · Topic 28

Reactions

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsD. AlkynesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alkyne reactions add twice (catalytic hydrogenation via Lindlar cis-alkene or Na/NH3 trans-alkene stops; halogen/HX double addition; hydration via HgSO4 to carbonyls - Markovnikov methyl ketones; hydroboration to aldehydes; oxidation cleavage; polymerisation to benzene/vinyl derivatives) plus terminal acidity (acetylide alkylations extending chains). Two pi bonds double addition stoichiometry - equivalents matter in quantitative problems.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Add twice ( Lindlar cis vs Na/NH3 trans control stereochemistry).
  • Hydrate to carbonyls; acetylides alkylate chains longer.
Remember
  • Lindlar gives cis; dissolving metal gives trans alkenes.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Acetylene on hydration (HgSO4/H2SO4) gives

Solution: Markovnikov hydration makes enol tautomerising to aldehyde.
Example 1.

Q. Propyne with 1 vs 2 moles of Br2. Give products.

  1. 1 mole: dibromopropene (one pi bond adds, E/Z mixture).
  2. 2 moles: 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane (both pi bonds saturate).
  3. Equivalents decide partial vs full addition.

Answer: Dibromopropene (1 eq) vs tetrabromopropane (2 eq).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.

Explanation

Concept. Addition of halogens to alkynes (Hydrocarbons, topic 32/41) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
Wurtz $2RX+2Na\\to R{-}R$; Finkelstein $RX+I^-\\to RI$; check selectivity first
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Addition of halogens to alkynes” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Chapter 3 · Topic 31

Nomenclature

HydrocarbonsHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsE. Aromatic hydrocarbonsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Aromatic nomenclature numbers to give substituents lowest locants (toluene methylbenzene, xylene dimethyl isomers o/m/p, phenol hydroxybenzene, aniline aminobenzene, benzaldehyde, benzoic acid - retained names) with o/m/p (1,2-/1,3-/1,4-) for disubstituted rings. Phenyl (C6H5-) versus benzyl (C6H5CH2-) prefixes distinguish ring-attached groups. Trivial names dominate commerce; IUPAC systematises exams.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Retained names (toluene, phenol, aniline) plus o/m/p positions.
  • Phenyl (ring) versus benzyl (ring-plus-CH2) prefixes.
Remember
  • o/m/p = 1,2- / 1,3- / 1,4- disubstitution shorthand.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

o/m/p notation in disubstituted benzenes means positions

Solution: Ortho-meta-para shorthand locates second substituents.
Example 1.

Q. Name C6H5-CH2Cl by two systems.

  1. IUPAC: (chloromethyl)benzene or phenylmethyl chloride systematically.
  2. Common: benzyl chloride.
  3. Benzyl (C6H5CH2-) vs phenyl (C6H5-) prefix distinction.

Answer: Benzyl chloride (common); (chloromethyl)benzene (IUPAC).

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Explanation

Concept. Side-chain chlorination (Aromatic Compounds, topic 18/30) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$IHD=(2C+2+N-H-X)/2$; $C_4H_{10}O$=7 (4 alcohols+3 ethers)
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).

Organic Compounds Containing Halogens

Haloalkanes and haloarenes: preparation, substitution, and famous compounds.

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

General
1. General2. Methods of preparation3. Properties4. Reactions5. Halo compounds6. Nature of C–X bond7. Substitution reactions8. Environmental effects9. Chloroform10. Iodoform11. Freons12. DDT

Deep Dive · Polar bonds, lively chemistry

Haloalkanes run preparation (alcohol-alkene routes plus Wurtz-Fittig-Finkelstein-Swarts-Grignard extras) and properties into substitution (SN1-SN2 with solvent-nucleophile-stereo extras, E1-E2 Saytzeff-Hofmann extras, reactivity orders, haloarene-benzyne extras) with famous compounds (chloroform, iodoform, freons, DDT plus important-compounds extras) carrying environmental weight (biomagnification, ozone loss, protocols). C-X polarity plus weakness explain everything; conditions choose SN versus elimination routes.
NEET facts:
  • Aqueous KOH substitutes (alcohols); alcoholic KOH eliminates (alkenes).
  • Chloroform makes phosgene in light-air; iodoform yellow-tests methyl ketones.
Fig: Same reagent, different solvent - substitution versus elimination switch.

Chapter 4 · Topic 1

General

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Haloalkanes and haloarenes (alkyl R-X, aryl Ar-X, vinyl, allyl, benzylic classes) centre C-X polarity (Cδ+-Xδ-; bond strength C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I dictating reactivity reverse) driving substitution-elimination chemistry. Classification (1°/2°/3° alkyl, allylic/benzylic resonance-activated, vinylic/aryl inert) predicts mechanism (SN1 favours stable cations; SN2 favours open back-sides). Halogen chemistry scales from solvents to war gases to drugs - same bonds, wide consequences.
NEET Snapshot:
  • C-X polarity plus bond-strength ladder govern reactivity.
  • I > Br > Cl >> F leaving order; allyl/benzyl activate.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

C-X bond strength order (strongest first) is

Solution: Shorter bonds bind tighter; reactivity runs reverse.

Chapter 4 · Topic 4

Reactions

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Haloalkane reactions branch substitution versus elimination: nucleophilic substitution (OH- alcohols, RO- ethers, CN- nitriles, NH3 amines, SH- thiols - solvent decides SN1/SN2), dehydrohalogenation (alcoholic KOH to alkenes, Saytzeff major), Wurtz coupling (Na to longer alkanes), Grignard formation (Mg/ether to RMgX reagents), Finkelstein-Swarts exchanges. Competing pathways (SN vs E, temperature-solvent controlled) make conditions decide products.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Substitute (nucleophiles), eliminate (alcoholic KOH), couple (Na), magnesiate (Mg).
  • Solvent-temperature choose SN versus E routes.
Haloalkane fates
PointDetail
Aqueous KOHAlcohols (substitution)
Alcoholic KOHAlkenes (elimination)
Na dry etherWurtz coupling
Mg dry etherGrignard reagents
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH mainly give

Solution: Alcoholic medium favours elimination over substitution.
Example 1.

Q. Chlorobenzene refuses SN1/SN2 but anisole substitutes easily. Contrast with alkyl halides.

  1. Aryl C-Cl: resonance double-bond character plus unstable phenyl cation block both mechanisms.
  2. Anisole ring activates electrophilic (not nucleophilic) substitution instead.
  3. Alkyl halides substitute nucleophilically; aryl halides resist (benzyne/dow only).

Answer: Alkyl SN1/SN2 works; aryl needs benzyne or Dow forcing.

Index / Hydrocarbons and Halogen Compounds
Chapter 4 · Topic 5

Halo compounds

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Halo compound classes (alkyl 1°/2°/3°, allylic/benzylic resonance-activated, vinylic/aryl inert, geminal/vicinal dihalides, trihaloform family) behave by structure: SN1 rates (allyl/benzyl/3° >> 2° > 1° > vinyl/aryl inert), SN2 rates (reverse: methyl > 1° > 2° >> 3°), eliminations need beta-hydrogens anti-periplanar. Classifying first predicts mechanism before drawing arrows - structure dictates pathway.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Alkyl/allyl/benzyl active; vinyl/aryl inert; gem/vicinal special.
  • SN1 favours stable cations; SN2 favours open backsides.
Remember
  • Classify halide first - mechanism follows structure.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most reactive toward SN1 among given is halide that is

Solution: Ionisation ease (cation stability) gates SN1 rates.
Example 1.

Q. Classify: CH3Cl, (CH3)3CCl, C6H5Cl, CH2=CHCl, C6H5CH2Cl.

  1. CH3Cl methyl, (CH3)3CCl tertiary alkyl; C6H5Cl aryl; CH2=CHCl vinyl; C6H5CH2Cl benzylic.
  2. Reactivity: benzylic/tert-alkyl fast SN1; vinyl/aryl inert; methyl fast SN2.
  3. Classify first - mechanism follows structure.

Answer: Methyl/tert/aryl/vinyl/benzylic classes with matching reactivity.

Nature of C–X bond

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

C-X bond nature (polar covalent: carbon δ+, halogen δ- by electronegativity gap; length grows F
NEET Snapshot:
  • Polar Cδ+-Xδ- with strength falling F to I.
  • Weak bases leave best (I- champion leaving group).
C-X bonds (kJ/mol)
PointDetail
C-F~485 (strongest, inert)
C-Cl~340
C-Br~285
C-I~240 (weakest, reactive)
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Best leaving group among halides is

Solution: Large diffuse iodide departs most willingly.
Example 1.

Q. C-F (485), C-Cl (340), C-Br (285), C-I (240 kJ/mol). Predict SN reactivity order and leaving-group order.

  1. Weaker bonds break faster: R-I > R-Br > R-Cl >> R-F.
  2. Leaving groups: I- > Br- > Cl- >> F- (weak bases leave best).
  3. Bond strength inversely tracks substitution speed.

Answer: I fastest, F slowest - weakness is reactivity.

Concept. SN2 mechanism (Halogen Derivatives, topic 5/29) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$rate=k[RX][Nu]$; backside inversion; $CH_3X>1^\\circ>2^\\circ$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Q. Two substrates on “Benzyne mechanism” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Environmental effects

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Halogen environmental effects cut both ways: DDT (persistent insecticide biomagnifying - eagle eggshell thinning, banned yet malaria-exceptional), freons/CFCs (refrigerant propellants destroying stratospheric ozone catalytically - Montreal Protocol phasing out), chloroform (anaesthetic turned hepatotoxic), halons (fire extinguishers depleting ozone). Persistence plus mobility magnify harm - Stockholm Convention targets POPs (persistent organic pollutants) globally.
NEET Snapshot:
  • DDT biomagnifies; CFCs deplete ozone; chloroform poisons liver.
  • Montreal Protocol heals ozone; Stockholm targets POPs.
Remember
  • Persistence plus mobility equals global pollutant.

Chapter 4 · Topic 9

Chloroform

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Chloroform (CHCl3: haloform from ethanol/acetone plus bleaching powder; anaesthetic historically, hepatotoxic/nephrotoxic plus phosgene-forming in light-air - brown bottles, ethanol stabiliser) tests carbylamine-positive (with primary amines) and silver-mirror negative. Lab preparation (chloral hydrate plus NaOH haloform reaction) demonstrates cleavage. Store dark with ethanol - light plus air make deadly phosgene.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Haloform-made anaesthetic turned liver poison.
  • Light-air makes phosgene; ethanol stabilises storage.
Remember
  • Brown bottles plus ethanol stabiliser prevent phosgene.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Chloroform on exposure to light and air forms poisonous gas

Solution: Photo-oxidation generates carbonyl chloride lethally.
Example 1.

Q. Why is chloroform stored in brown bottles with ethanol?

  1. Light + air oxidise CHCl3 to deadly phosgene (COCl2).
  2. Brown glass blocks light; ethanol converts phosgene to harmless diethyl carbonate.
  3. Storage discipline prevents poisoning.

Answer: Phosgene prevention: dark bottles plus ethanol stabiliser.

Chapter 4 · Topic 10

Iodoform

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Iodoform (CHI3 yellow antiseptic-smelling precipitate) tests methyl ketones and ethanol/secondary methyl alcohols (I2/NaOH haloform: yellow ppt confirms CH3CO- or CH3CHOH- groups) - acetophenone positive, benzophenone negative (no methyl). Mechanism (tri-iodination then hydroxide cleavage) generalises to chloroform/bromoform with respective halogens. Antiseptic history (dressings) plus analytical use double its fame.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Yellow precipitate diagnoses methyl ketones/ethanol.
  • Haloform cleavage (I2/OH-) generalises to Cl/Br analogues.
Remember
  • Acetophenone positive (methyl); benzophenone negative (phenyl).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Iodoform test is positive for compound containing group

Solution: Methyl carbonyls cleave to yellow CHI3 diagnostically.
Example 1.

Q. Acetophenone gives yellow CHI3 with I2/NaOH; benzophenone gives nothing. Explain.

  1. Acetophenone has COCH3 (methyl ketone) - tri-iodination then cleavage yields iodoform.
  2. Benzophenone (COPh2) lacks methyl - no haloform cleavage possible.
  3. Methyl carbonyl is the haloform structural ticket.

Answer: CH3CO- present vs absent decides yellow precipitate.

Chapter 4 · Topic 11

Freons

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Freons (CFCs: CCl2F2 Freon-12 refrigerants, propellants, blowing agents - non-toxic, non-flammable, ultra-stable) persist to stratosphere where UV releases chlorine catalytically destroying ozone (one atom kills 100,000 O3) - Montreal Protocol (1987, universal) phases them to HFCs/HFOs (no chlorine). Antarctic ozone hole each spring visualises damage; healing spots now appearing - policy triumph proving cooperation works.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Stable refrigerants releasing ozone-killing chlorine aloft.
  • Montreal Protocol replaces CFCs with HFCs/HFOs.
Remember
  • One chlorine atom destroys 100,000 ozone molecules.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Freons deplete stratospheric ozone by releasing

Solution: UV-liberated chlorine cycles ozone destruction repeatedly.
Example 1.

Q. CFCs were ideal refrigerants yet got banned. Explain the paradox.

  1. Ideal below: non-toxic, non-flammable, stable (safe handling).
  2. Deadly above: UV releases chlorine catalytically destroying ozone (one atom kills 100,000 O3).
  3. Stability (virtue below) becomes persistence (vice above).

Answer: Safe handling but stratospheric ozone destruction - banned by Montreal Protocol.

Chapter 4 · Topic 12

DDT

Organic Compounds Containing HalogensHydrocarbons and Halogen CompoundsGeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane: chloral plus chlorobenzene, contact insecticide - Nobel Muller 1948) saved millions from malaria-typhus then biomagnified (fat-stored, persistent: eagle eggshell thinning, human milk residues) earning bans (Stockholm POP listing) with malaria-country exemptions. First-generation organochlorine lesson: persistence plus mobility equals global pollution - IPM plus bednets replace blanket spraying.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Malaria-saver turned biomagnifying pollutant.
  • Banned broadly, exempted for malaria control.
Remember
  • Eggshell thinning proved biomagnification visibly.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

DDT was banned mainly due to

Solution: Fat-stored DDT concentrated up food chains catastrophically.
Example 1.

Q. DDT saved millions from malaria yet was banned in most uses. Explain both sides.

  1. Saves: kills mosquito vectors cheaply, persistently (Nobel Muller 1948).
  2. Costs: biomagnifies (fat-stored, eagle eggshell thinning, human milk residues).
  3. Malaria-country exemptions balance lives today versus wildlife tomorrow.

Answer: Vector-killing benefit versus biomagnification cost.

Deep Dive · Oxygen functional ladder

Oxygen compounds climb oxidation states: alcohols (types with Lucas-oxidation-dehydration diagnostics, preparations from alkenes-Grignards-carbonyls) to phenols (cumene/diazonium preparations, resonance acidity, electrophilic substitutions with Reimer-Tiemann-Kolbe extras) to ethers (Williamson preparations, HI cleavage, anisole chemistry) to carbonyls (structure-nomenclature-preparation extras, nucleophilic addition with HCN-Grignard-ammonia extras, oxidation with Tollens-Fehlings extras, reductions with Clemmensen-Wolff-Kishner extras, alpha-H acidity with keto-enol extras, aldol-Claisen, Cannizzaro, haloform with iodoform extras). Oxidation level decides class; reagents climb or descend ladders.
NEET facts:
  • Lucas instant/slow/none = 3°/2°/1° alcohols; Tollens/Fehlings oxidise aldehydes only.
  • Aldol needs alpha-H; Cannizzaro needs none; haloform needs methyl carbonyls.
Fig: Oxidise alcohols up to acids; reduce back down - ladder traversable both ways.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Tollens and Fehling tests distinguish aldehydes from ketones because they oxidise

Solution: Mild oxidants convert aldehydes (H present), not ketones.

Chapter 5 · Topic 1

Methods of preparation

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsA. GeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Oxygen-compound preparations share routes: alcohols (alkene hydration, haloalkane hydrolysis, Grignard-carbonyl, fermentation), phenols (cumene, diazonium hydrolysis, Dow alkali fusion), ethers (Williamson, dehydration), aldehydes-ketones (alcohol oxidation, ozonolysis, Rosenmund/Stephen reductions, Friedel-Crafts acylation). Hydration-hydrolysis-oxidation trio covers most entries - preparation logic follows functional-group interconversion ladders.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Hydration, hydrolysis, oxidation, reduction interconvert classes.
  • Grignard plus Rosenmund/Stephen build carbonyls specifically.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Phenol is industrially prepared mainly via process called

Solution: Cumene oxidation plus acid cleavage yields phenol plus acetone.
Example 1.

Q. Prepare ethanol from ethene and from bromoethane.

  1. Ethene plus conc. H2SO4 (oxonium intermediate) then hydrolysis gives ethanol (Markovnikov hydration).
  2. Bromoethane plus aqueous KOH (SN2, OH- replaces Br) gives ethanol.
  3. Hydration adds water across double bonds; hydrolysis substitutes halides.

Answer: Acid hydration of ethene; aqueous-KOH substitution of bromoethane.

Chapter 5 · Topic 2

Properties

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsA. GeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Oxygen-compound properties track hydrogen bonding: alcohols-phenols (high boiling, water-soluble small members, acidic phenols vs neutral alcohols), ethers (volatile, water-miscible small, inert solvents), aldehydes-ketones (polar carbonyls, lower boiling than H-bonding analogues, water-soluble small). Boiling trends (acids > alcohols > aldehydes > ethers ≈ alkanes) mirror H-bonding strength directly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • H-bonding decides boiling and solubility trends.
  • Acids > alcohols > carbonyls > ethers boiling order.
Remember
  • Phenols acidic (resonance); alcohols neutral; ethers inert solvents.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Highest boiling among ethanol, ethanal, ethane and dimethyl ether is

Solution: Hydrogen-bonded alcohols outboil polar aprotic analogues.
Example 1.

Q. Ethanol (bp 78C) vs dimethyl ether (bp -24C), same formula C2H6O. Explain.

  1. Ethanol H-bonds (O-H donors) associating strongly - high boiling.
  2. Dimethyl ether cannot donate H-bonds - weak dipoles only, gaseous.
  3. Functional group decides intermolecular forces, hence boiling points.

Answer: H-bonding ethanol boils high; non-H-bonding ether stays gaseous.

Chapter 5 · Topic 3

Reactions

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsA. GeneralStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Oxygen-compound reactions branch by group: alcohols (acidic proton, nucleophilic substitution via protonation, elimination to alkenes, oxidation ladder), phenols (acidic, electrophilic substitution activated, Reimer-Tiemann/Kolbe carboxylations), ethers (HI cleavage, electrophilic anisole substitution), carbonyls (nucleophilic addition, α-chemistry, oxidation-reduction). Group recognition predicts pathways - classify first, mechanism follows.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Alcohols substitute/eliminate/oxidise; phenols activate rings; carbonyls add.
  • Ethers cleave with HI; anisole substitutes activated.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Lucas test (conc. HCl/ZnCl2 turbidity speed) distinguishes classes of

Solution: Carbocation stability orders turbidity appearance rates.
Example 1.

Q. Phenol (acidic) vs ethanol (neutral) vs Lucas (turbidity) vs FeCl3 (violet): design an identification scheme for three bottles.

  1. FeCl3 violet identifies phenol (phenolic OH only).
  2. Lucas test on remainder: instant turbidity (3°), slow (2°), none (1° ethanol).
  3. Ceric ammonium nitrate red confirms alcoholic OH backup.

Answer: FeCl3 finds phenol; Lucas times alcohol class; ceric confirms.

Chapter 5 · Topic 4

Types

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsB. AlcoholsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alcohol types by carbon bearing OH: primary (1°, one carbon neighbour - oxidise to aldehydes then acids), secondary (2°, ketones on oxidation), tertiary (3°, resist oxidation, dehydrate fastest via stable cations). Lucas test (instant/slow/none turbidity), oxidation products (aldehyde/ketone/none) and dehydration rates (3°>2°>1°) classify unknowns practically. Type decides every alcohol reaction outcome.
NEET Snapshot:
  • 1° oxidise fully, 2° to ketones, 3° resist (dehydrate fastest).
  • Lucas plus oxidation plus dehydration triangulate type.
Alcohol types
PointDetail
PrimaryAldehyde then acid on oxidation
SecondaryKetone on oxidation
TertiaryResists oxidation; dehydrates fastest
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Tertiary alcohols on oxidation give

Solution: No alpha-hydrogen blocks oxidation; elimination proceeds.
Example 1.

Q. Methanol, ethanol, isopropanol, tert-butanol: classify and predict Lucas behaviour.

  1. Methanol, ethanol: primary (no turbidity cold).
  2. Isopropanol: secondary (turbidity in minutes).
  3. tert-Butanol: tertiary (instant turbidity).
  4. Carbon count on OH-bearing carbon classifies; carbocation stability times Lucas.

Answer: 1° (none), 2° (slow), 3° (instant) Lucas responses.

Chapter 5 · Topic 5

Primary alcohols

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsB. AlcoholsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Primary alcohols (R-CH2OH: ethanol, methanol) oxidise stepwise (aldehyde then acid with strong agents; aldehyde stop with PCC), dehydrate slowest (least-stable primary cations), undergo SN2 readily (unhindered backside), and form esters smoothly. Fermentation (ethanol), wood spirit (methanol, toxic blindness-causing), and Lucas silence (no turbidity cold) mark the class. Fuel, solvent and beverage roles dominate commerce.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Oxidise fully; dehydrate slowest; SN2 readily; Lucas silent.
  • Ethanol (fermentation) and methanol (wood spirit) headline.
Remember
  • Methanol blinds; ethanol intoxicates - dose and type matter.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Primary alcohols with PCC (mild oxidant) stop at

Solution: Controlled oxidation halts at aldehyde stage.
Example 1.

Q. Distinguish 1-propanol from 2-propanol chemically.

  1. Oxidise both with acidified K2Cr2O7: 1-propanol gives propanoic acid (via propanal); 2-propanol gives acetone (ketone, stops).
  2. Confirm: Tollens oxidises propanal (silver mirror), not acetone.
  3. Oxidation ceiling (acid vs ketone) plus Tollens splits primary/secondary.

Answer: Propanoic acid + Tollens-positive (1°) vs acetone + Tollens-negative (2°).

Back to Index
Index / Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds
Chapter 5 · Topic 6

Secondary alcohols

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsB. AlcoholsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Secondary alcohols (R2CHOH: isopropanol rubbing alcohol) oxidise to ketones only (no further without C-C cleavage), dehydrate middling (secondary cations), Lucas-turbid slowly (minutes), and esterify moderately. Rubbing alcohol antisepsis plus industrial solvent roles dominate uses. Ketone products resist further oxidation - class ceiling defines the chemistry.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Oxidise to ketones and stop; Lucas slow; dehydrate middling.
  • Isopropanol antiseptic plus solvent roles.
Remember
  • Ketone ceiling caps secondary oxidation.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Isopropanol on strong oxidation gives

Solution: Secondary oxidation halts at ketone stage.
Example 1.

Q. 2-Butanol on oxidation gives a ketone that resists further oxidation. Identify and explain.

  1. Secondary alcohol oxidises to butan-2-one (ketone).
  2. Ketones lack alpha-H-free? No - they have alpha-H but no H on carbonyl carbon, so mild oxidants stop.
  3. Secondary ceiling is ketone; primary goes to acid.

Answer: Butan-2-one - ketones resist mild oxidation without aldehydic H.

Index / Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds
Chapter 5 · Topic 7

Tertiary alcohols

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsB. AlcoholsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Tertiary alcohols (R3COH) resist oxidation (no alpha-H), dehydrate fastest (stable 3° cations, Saytzeff alkenes), Lucas-instant (turbidity immediately), and eliminate rather than substitute. Glycerol? no - tert-butanol fuel oxygenate plus lab hindered base contexts. Stability inverts reactivity versus primary across oxidation, dehydration and substitution modes.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Resist oxidation; dehydrate fastest; Lucas instant.
  • Stable cations flip all primary trends.
Remember
  • 3° always fastest where cations form, slowest where SN2 needs space.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Lucas test gives immediate turbidity with alcohols that are

Solution: Instant carbocation formation clouds tertiary samples at once.
Example 1.

Q. tert-Pentyl alcohol with conc. H2SO4 (heat) gives major alkene. Predict it.

  1. Protonate OH, leave as water: stable 3° carbocation forms instantly.
  2. Eliminate beta-H following Saytzeff (most substituted alkene): 2-methylbut-2-ene major.
  3. Stable cations plus Saytzeff orientation decide.

Answer: 2-Methylbut-2-ene (Saytzeff, via 3° cation).

Chapter 5 · Topic 10

Reactions

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsB. AlcoholsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alcohol reactions: acidic proton (Na/H2 evolution, alkoxides), nucleophilic substitution (HX/ZnCl2 Lucas, PCl5/SOCl2 to halides, protonated-OH leaving), elimination (conc. H2SO4 to alkenes Saytzeff, 3°>2°>1°), oxidation ladder (1° to acids, 2° to ketones, 3° resists), esterification (acids to esters), Lucas/dehydration diagnostics. Protonate-then-substitute-or-eliminate logic unifies alcohol chemistry.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Acidic H, substitution (Lucas), elimination (Saytzeff), oxidation ladder.
  • Protonated OH leaves; carbocation stability decides routes.
Alcohol fates
PointDetail
HX/ZnCl2Alkyl halides (Lucas rates 3>2>1)
Conc. H2SO4Alkenes (Saytzeff)
Strong [O]Acids/ketones/nothing by type
AcidsEsters

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 5 · Topic 12

Preparation

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsC. PhenolsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phenol preparations: cumene process (industrial: oxidation plus acid cleavage with acetone co-product), diazonium hydrolysis (warm aqueous, N2 released), Dow process (chlorobenzene fused NaOH, high T/P), coal-tar extraction (historic), benzene sulphonic acid fusion. Cumene dominates commerce (acetone bonus); diazonium routes serve labs. Alkali fusion of sulphonates is textbook classic.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Cumene industrial; diazonium lab; Dow fusion classic.
  • Coal-tar extraction sourced phenol historically.
Remember
  • Cumene route pays acetone bonus alongside phenol.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Industrial phenol is mainly made via process called

Solution: Isopropylbenzene oxidation plus cleavage scales cheapest.
Example 1.

Q. Cumene process makes phenol plus which co-product? Write the significance.

  1. Isopropylbenzene oxidised to hydroperoxide, acid-cleaved to phenol plus acetone.
  2. Acetone co-product funds the process economically.
  3. Dual-product economics make cumene route dominant.

Answer: Acetone - valuable co-product subsidising phenol manufacture.

Chapter 5 · Topic 13

Properties

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsC. PhenolsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Phenol properties: crystalline (carbolic acid misnomer - weak acid), antiseptic (Lister sprays, low solubility), steam-volatile (o-nitrophenol H-bonding intramolecular), corrosive burns, FeCl3 violet complex diagnostic. Acidity (pKa ~10, resonance-stabilised phenoxide) beats alcohols million-fold yet trails carboxylic acids. электронного effects tune (nitro strengthens, methyl weakens) - substituent logic throughout.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Weak acid (resonance phenoxide), antiseptic, FeCl3 violet.
  • Million-fold more acidic than alcohols.
Remember
  • Nitro groups strengthen; alkyl groups weaken phenol acidity.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Phenol gives violet colour with reagent

Solution: Phenol-iron complexes diagnose phenolic groups.
Example 1.

Q. Phenol (pKa ~10) vs ethanol (pKa ~16) vs water (15.7): explain the acidity ladder.

  1. Phenoxide resonance-delocalises negative charge into ring (stabilised conjugate base).
  2. Ethoxide has no resonance (charge localised, unstable).
  3. Resonance stabilisation makes phenol a million-fold more acidic.

Answer: Phenoxide resonance vs localised ethoxide explains 10^6 gap.

Index / Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds
Chapter 5 · Topic 16

Structure

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsD. EthersStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Ether structure (R-O-R bent ~110°, polar C-O bonds cancelling partially, no O-H donors) gives volatility (low boiling), water-miscibility small members (H-bond accepting), inertness (few reactions - ideal solvents: diethyl ether, THF, dioxane), and peroxide hazards (aged ethers explode on distillation - ferrous test, nitrogen storage). Crown ethers trap cations selectively (phase-transfer catalysis). Bent polar aprotic character defines ether behaviour.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Bent, polar-aprotic, H-accepting, inert - ideal solvents.
  • Peroxide formation endangers old ether bottles.
Remember
  • Test old ethers for peroxides before distilling ever.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Diethyl ether is an excellent solvent because it is

Solution: Dissolving power without reacting suits Grignard chemistry.
Example 1.

Q. Diethyl ether structure is bent (~110°) yet almost non-polar in behaviour. Explain.

  1. Bent C-O-C with two lone pairs; bond dipoles partially cancel (net ~1.2 D, small).
  2. No O-H donors: cannot H-bond donate, only accept weakly - volatile, inert solvent.
  3. Geometry plus no-donor status make ethers ideal Grignard solvents.

Answer: Bent polar-aprotic structure: dissolving power without reacting.

Explanation

Concept. Williamson synthesis (Alcohols and Ethers, topic 11/26) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
Wurtz $2RX+2Na\\to R{-}R$; Finkelstein $RX+I^-\\to RI$; check selectivity first
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Chapter 5 · Topic 20

Carbonyl group

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsE. Aldehydes and KetonesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Carbonyl group (C=O polarised: carbon δ+, oxygen δ-; planar sp2; pi bond exposed) drives nucleophilic addition (attack carbon), acidity of alpha-hydrogens (enolate resonance), and IR stretch (~1715 cm-1 diagnostic). Aldehydes (R-CHO, oxidisable) versus ketones (R2C=O, resistant) split by hydrogen presence. Formaldehyde (preservative), acetone (solvent), benzaldehyde (almond) industrial faces.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Polar planar pi bond: nucleophiles attack carbon.
  • Aldehydes oxidise; ketones resist - hydrogen decides.
Remember
  • IR ~1715 cm-1 barcodes carbonyl groups.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Aldehydes differ from ketones in being

Solution: Aldehydic hydrogen oxidises to acids; ketones lack it.
Example 1.

Q. Formaldehyde (gas) vs acetaldehyde (volatile liquid) vs benzaldehyde (liquid): explain trend.

  1. Mass rises (30, 44, 106) strengthening dispersion forces.
  2. All lack H-bond donation (no O-H); dipole interactions dominate.
  3. Benzaldehyde extra aromatic stacking raises boiling further.

Answer: Mass plus pi-stacking climb boiling formaldehyde to benzaldehyde.

Index / Oxygen and Nitrogen Compounds
Chapter 5 · Topic 21

Structure

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsE. Aldehydes and KetonesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Carbonyl structure (trigonal planar ~120°, pi cloud above-below, dipole ~2.7 D) invites nucleophilic attack trajectories (Bürgi-Dunitz ~107° angles) - sterics (bulky groups slow) plus electronics (donors deactivate, withdrawers activate) tune rates. Formaldehyde (most reactive, no donors), aromatic aldehydes (conjugated, milder), hindered ketones (slowest) rank reactivity. Structure predicts addition speed directly.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Planar polar carbonyls attacked at Bürgi-Dunitz angles.
  • Formaldehyde fastest; hindered ketones slowest.
Remember
  • Electron donors deactivate; withdrawers activate carbonyls.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Most reactive carbonyl toward nucleophilic addition is

Solution: Unhindered undonated carbonyl accepts fastest.

Explanation

Concept. Reactions of aldehydes and ketones (Carbonyl Compounds, topic 13/32) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
Compare resonance $>$ hyperconjugation $>$ $+I$; $-I$ falls with distance
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Reactions of aldehydes and ketones” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 5 · Topic 27

Acidity of α-hydrogen

Organic Compounds Containing OxygenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsE. Aldehydes and KetonesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Alpha-hydrogen acidity (carbonyl-adjacent C-H, pKa ~20, enolate resonance-stabilised) enables aldol condensations (enolate plus carbonyl), haloform cleavage (triple-halogenated methyl ketones), HVZ bromination (P/Br2 acids), and racemisation (chiral centres enolise). No alpha-H (formaldehyde, benzaldehyde, pivaldehyde) diverts to Cannizzaro instead - hydrogen presence routes mechanisms. Acidity mild yet synthetically mighty.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Alpha-H enolises enabling aldol, haloform, HVZ routes.
  • No alpha-H diverts to Cannizzaro disproportionation.
Remember
  • Alpha-H presence decides aldol versus Cannizzaro fates.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Aldol condensation needs carbonyls with

Solution: Enolate nucleophiles require abstractable alpha protons.

Organic Compounds Containing Nitrogen

Amines with basicity ladders and diazonium salts for synthesis.

Organic Compounds Containing NitrogenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsChapter Introduction

Subtopics in this Chapter

A. Amines
1. Preparation2. Properties3. Reactions4. Nomenclature5. Classification6. Structure7. Basic character
B. Diazonium salts
8. Preparation/basic chemistry9. Properties/reactions relevant to syllabus10. Importance in synthetic organic chemistry

Deep Dive · Nitrogen bases to dye makers

Nitrogen chemistry runs amines (nomenclature-classification-structure basics; preparations via reductions, Gabriel, Hoffmann; properties; basicity ladders with structural extras; reactions with carbylamine-Hinsberg-alkylation-acylation-nitrous extras) into diazonium salts (cold preparation with mechanism extras, Sandmeyer-Gattermann-Schiemann-azo-coupling properties, synthetic importance). Basicity (alkyl up, aryl down, solvation reshuffles) plus diazonium versatility (swap, couple, deaminate) carry most marks.
NEET facts:
  • Carbylamine (foul) proves primary amines; Hinsberg separates 1°/2°/3°.
  • Cold diazotisation (0-5°C) then warm reactions - temperature discipline matters.
Fig: Alkyl donation beats ammonia beats aryl delocalisation (aqueous).

Chapter 6 · Topic 4

Nomenclature

Organic Compounds Containing NitrogenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsA. AminesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Amine nomenclature: common (alkylamine: ethylamine, aniline, toluidine) versus IUPAC (alkanamine: ethanamine, benzenamine; N-substitution tagged N-methyl, N,N-dimethyl). Primary/secondary/tertiary classify by carbons on nitrogen (versus alcohols which count differently - longest chain rule). Aryl (aniline) versus alkyl versus heterocyclic (pyridine, pyrrole) families name separately. N-locants clarify substituted nitrogens always.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Common alkylamine versus IUPAC alkanamine systems.
  • N-prefix tags nitrogen substituents explicitly.
Remember
  • Amine 1°/2°/3° counts carbons on nitrogen.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

IUPAC name of ethylamine is

Solution: Two-carbon amine names ethanamine systematically.
Example 1.

Q. Name CH3-NH-CH2CH3 by common and IUPAC systems.

  1. Common: ethylmethylamine (alkyls alphabetical).
  2. IUPAC: N-methylethanamine (parent ethane, N-methyl tag).
  3. Secondary amine naming in both dialects.

Answer: Ethylmethylamine (common); N-methylethanamine (IUPAC).

Classification

Organic Compounds Containing NitrogenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsA. AminesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Explanation

Concept. Classification and nomenclature (Amines, topic 1/24) is a high-weight NEET idea. First classify the substrate (degree, conjugation, alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain), then select the electron effect and mechanism path before writing the product.
Key formula / trend to memorise
$sp^3$ $109.5^\\circ$, $sp^2$ $120^\\circ$, $sp$ $180^\\circ$; $DBE=C-H/2+N/2+1$
Make this a one-line flashcard. Most NEET MCQs test exactly this order or transformation.
Key points.
  • Classify: degree, conjugation, presence of alpha-H, leaving group, ring vs chain.
  • Choose effect: -I/+I for distance polarity; -M/+M and resonance for conjugated systems; hyperconjugation for carbocation and alkene stability.
  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “Classification and nomenclature” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Chapter 6 · Topic 6

Structure

Organic Compounds Containing NitrogenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsA. AminesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Amine structure (pyramidal nitrogen with lone pair: rapid inversion racemising most amines, quaternary salts locked tetrahedral) decides basicity (lone pair availability) and geometry. Alkyl groups push electron density up (stronger bases gas-phase); aryl delocalisation drains it (aniline weak); aqueous solvation reshuffles orders (ammonium ion stability matters). Hydrogen bonding (1°/2° associate, 3° cannot donate) sets boiling trends.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Pyramidal inverting nitrogen with basic lone pair.
  • Alkyl pushes up, aryl drains, solvation reshuffles basicity.
Remember
  • Rapid inversion prevents chiral amine isolation (usually).
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Amines are basic due to

Solution: Available lone pairs accept protons defining basicity.
Example 1.

Q. Trimethylamine (tertiary) boils lower than methylamine (primary) despite higher mass. Why?

  1. Primary amines H-bond (N-H donors) associating strongly.
  2. Tertiary amines lack N-H donors (no H-bonding among themselves).
  3. H-bonding ability beats mass in boiling trends.

Answer: N-H donors associate; tertiary amines cannot self-bond.

Chapter 6 · Topic 10

Importance in synthetic organic chemistry

Organic Compounds Containing NitrogenOxygen and Nitrogen CompoundsB. Diazonium saltsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Diazonium importance crowns synthetic organic chemistry: Sandmeyer-Gattermann (Cl/Br/CN swaps), Schiemann (F via fluoroborate), azo coupling (dyes with phenols/amines - methyl orange, Congo red), reduction (deamination via hypophosphorous acid), plus phenol synthesis (warm hydrolysis). Dye industry (azo colours), indicators and medicine run on diazonium versatility - cold-prepared, warm-deployed workhorse intermediates.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sandmeyer swaps, coupling dyes, reduction deaminates.
  • Dye industry plus indicators run on diazonium chemistry.
Diazonium uses
PointDetail
Sandmeyer/GattermannCl/Br/CN replacements
Azo couplingDyes with phenols/amines
Warm waterPhenols
H3PO2Deamination (remove NH2)
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Azo coupling of diazonium salts with phenols gives

Solution: N=N-linked chromophores dye textiles and indicators.
Example 1.

Q. Aniline plus NaNO2/HCl (0-5C) then warm water gives which product? Write the sequence.

  1. Cold diazotisation: aniline to benzenediazonium chloride.
  2. Warm hydrolysis replaces N2+ with OH: phenol forms.
  3. Diazonium route converts aryl amines to phenols cleanly.

Answer: Phenol via benzenediazonium intermediate.

Carbohydrates, proteins, vitamins, nucleic acids and hormones.

Deep Dive · Molecules of life and medicine

Biomolecules run carbohydrates (classification with polysaccharide extras, aldoses-ketoses specifics, monosaccharides with glucose-Fischer-Haworth-anomer-mutarotation-epimer extras, oligosaccharides with glycosidic-reducing extras) through proteins (amino acids with zwitterion-isoelectric-essential extras, peptide-polypeptide links, structures with primary-secondary-tertiary extras, denaturation) into vitamins (classification plus functions), nucleic acids (DNA-RNA structures-functions with nucleoside-base-pairing extras) and hormones (general signalling with pairs). Fuel, builders, archives and regulators - life chemistry complete.
NEET facts:
  • Benedict reduces sugars; Biuret violets proteins; Sudan oranges fats.
  • DNA archives double-helix; RNA acts single-stranded (U for T).
Fig: Sugars fuel, proteins build, nucleic acids archive - life chemistry trio.

Solution: Copper complexes peptide bonds turning violet.

Index / Biomolecules and Practical Chemistry
Chapter 7 · Topic 1

Biomolecules

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryA. IntroductionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Biomolecules (carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, vitamins, hormones - carbon chemistry running life) divide fuels (sugars, fats), builders (proteins), messengers (hormones, nucleotides) and archives (DNA/RNA). Structure decides function at every scale (glucose fuel, haemoglobin carriage, DNA storage). Biochemistry reads life as coordinated organic reactions - metabolism is organic chemistry inside cells.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Carbs fuel, proteins build, nucleic acids archive, vitamins-hormones regulate.
  • Structure-function logic governs every biomolecule.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Biomolecules include all EXCEPT

Solution: Inert gases play no biochemical roles.
Example 1.

Q. Classify: glucose, haemoglobin, DNA, vitamin C, insulin.

  1. Glucose: carbohydrate (monosaccharide fuel).
  2. Haemoglobin: protein (oxygen transport). DNA: nucleic acid (archive).
  3. Vitamin C: vitamin (antioxidant cofactor). Insulin: protein hormone (peptide signal).
  4. Class by chemistry plus role: fuel, builder, archive, helper, signal.

Answer: Carb, protein, nucleic acid, vitamin, peptide hormone respectively.

Back to Index
Index / Biomolecules and Practical Chemistry
Chapter 7 · Topic 2

Importance of biomolecules

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryA. IntroductionStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Biomolecules matter because life IS their chemistry: energy (ATP-glucose-fatty oxidation), structure (cellulose walls, keratin skin, collagen tendon), information (DNA inheritance, RNA messaging), regulation (hormones, vitamins as coenzymes), defence (antibodies). Malnutrition (protein-energy, vitamin deficiencies), diabetes (insulin-glucose failure) and cancer (DNA damage) are biomolecule disorders - medicine treats molecules.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Energy, structure, information, regulation, defence - life functions.
  • Malnutrition, diabetes, cancer are molecule-level diseases.
Remember
  • You are what your molecules do - biochemistry is fate.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Diabetes mellitus is a disorder of biomolecule metabolism involving

Solution: Insulin-glucose axis failure defines diabetes.
Example 1.

Q. Why are vitamins needed in milligrams while carbs in grams?

  1. Vitamins act catalytically (coenzymes recycled per reaction).
  2. Carbs burn stoichiometrically as fuel (consumed per ATP).
  3. Catalysts recycle; fuels combust - dosage follows chemistry.

Answer: Coenzyme recycling needs traces; fuel burning needs bulk.

Chapter 7 · Topic 4

Aldoses

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryB. CarbohydratesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Aldoses (aldehyde sugars: glyceraldehyde triose, ribose pentose, glucose hexose) reduce Tollens/Fehling/Benedict (free -CHO oxidises), form osazones (phenylhydrazine crystals identifying sugars), and cyclise to hemiacetals (pyranose/furanose rings dominating in solution). D/L assignment follows lowest-chiral-centre OH (right = D, left = L) - most natural sugars D-form. Glyceraldehyde standards anchor all carbohydrate stereochemistry.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Aldehyde sugars reducing Tollens/Fehling/Benedict.
  • D/L by lowest-centre OH; most natural sugars D.
Remember
  • Osazone crystal shapes identified sugars classically.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Glucose is an aldose because it contains group

Solution: Terminal -CHO reduces tests and cyclises to hemiacetals.
Example 1.

Q. Glucose (aldohexose) vs fructose (ketohexose): two distinguishing tests.

  1. Seliwanoff (resorcinol/HCl): fructose rapid red, glucose slow.
  2. Osazone crystals differ (glucosazone vs fructosazone melting shapes).
  3. Both reduce Benedict (fructose via alkaline isomerisation).

Answer: Seliwanoff speed plus osazone shapes split aldose/ketose.

Back to Index
Index / Biomolecules and Practical Chemistry
Chapter 7 · Topic 5

Ketoses

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryB. CarbohydratesStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Ketoses (ketone sugars: dihydroxyacetone triose, ribulose pentose, fructose hexose) reduce tests only after Lobry-de Bruyn rearrangement (alkaline isomerisation to aldoses) - Seliwanoff resorcinol test (rapid red for ketoses) distinguishes directly. Fructose (fruit sugar, sweetest) plus ribulose (Calvin CO2 acceptor) headline roles. Furanose rings dominate ketose cyclisation (five-membered).
NEET Snapshot:
  • Ketone sugars; Seliwanoff red diagnoses rapidly.
  • Fructose sweetest; ribulose fixes Calvin carbon.
Remember
  • Alkaline isomerisation lets ketoses reduce tests indirectly.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Seliwanoff test (rapid red) diagnoses sugars that are

Solution: Keto-sugars dehydrate faster to furfurals colouring resorcinol.
Example 1.

Q. Honey (fructose-rich) tastes sweeter than glucose syrup. Explain.

  1. Fructose is the sweetest natural sugar (furanose ketose).
  2. Glucose less sweet; sucrose intermediate (50% fructose).
  3. Ketose structure plus receptor fit maximise sweetness.

Answer: Fructose sweetness tops glucose and sucrose.

  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.

Chapter 7 · Topic 9

Peptide bond

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryC. ProteinsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Peptide bonds (C-N links between amino acid carboxyl and amino groups, water lost - rigid planar partial-double character) chain residues N-to-C directionally: dipeptides, oligopeptides (glutathione antioxidant tripeptide), polypeptides (insulin 51 residues, two chains). Ribosomes form (peptidyl transferase rRNA catalyses); proteases digest specifically (trypsin after basic residues). Primary structure is peptide-bond order - sequencing reads it.
NEET Snapshot:
  • C-N links chaining residues N-to-C directionally.
  • Ribosomes make; proteases cut specifically.
Remember
  • Partial-double character stiffens peptide backbones.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Peptide bonds form between amino acids with loss of

Solution: Carboxyl-plus-amino condensation builds chains.
Example 1.

Q. Gly-Gly dipeptide: draw the linkage and name the bond.

  1. Two glycines condense (COOH + NH2 minus H2O).
  2. C-N link with partial-double rigidity is the peptide bond.
  3. N-to-C direction: glycylglycine.

Answer: Peptide (amide) bond linking N to C directionally.

Index / Biomolecules and Practical Chemistry
Chapter 7 · Topic 10

Polypeptides

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryC. ProteinsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Polypeptides (10-100 residue chains: insulin, glucagon, oxytocin nanomers; growth hormone longer) bridge peptides to proteins - length plus folding decides naming, not sharp cutoffs. Solid-phase synthesis (Merrifield, C-to-N stepwise on resins) builds custom peptides (drugs: vasopressin analogues, GLP-1 agonists); native ligation joins fragments. Therapeutic peptides (injectable, gut-unstable) balance specificity against delivery limits.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Medium chains bridging peptides to proteins.
  • Merrifield solid-phase synthesis builds to order.
Remember
  • Insulin (51 residues) sits at peptide-protein border.
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Insulin contains amino-acid residues numbering

Solution: Two-chain 51-residue polypeptide defines therapeutic protein.
Example 1.

Q. Oxytocin (9 residues) vs haemoglobin (574 residues): which is polypeptide vs protein?

  1. Oxytocin: oligopeptide (few residues, hormone signal).
  2. Haemoglobin: protein (tetramer, cooperative oxygen carriage).
  3. Length plus folding complexity grades peptide to protein.

Answer: Oxytocin oligopeptide; haemoglobin full protein.

Chapter 7 · Topic 11

Protein structure

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryC. ProteinsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Protein structure levels (primary sequence, secondary helices-sheets via H-bonds, tertiary 3D via disulphide-hydrophobic-ionic contacts, quaternary subunit assemblies) build function hierarchically - haemoglobin tetramer cooperativity, enzyme active-site pockets, keratin coiled coils, silk stacked sheets. Denaturation unravels 2°-4° (function dies, sequence survives); chaperones assist folding; misfolding aggregates cause Alzheimer-prion diseases.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Sequence to motifs to folds to assemblies - hierarchy builds function.
  • Denaturation kills shape, spares sequence.

PrimaryAmino-acid order
SecondaryHelices, sheets (H-bonds)
Tertiary3D fold (S-S, hydrophobic)
QuaternarySubunit assembly

Chapter 7 · Topic 14

Functions

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryD. VitaminsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

Vitamin functions (B-complex coenzymes: B1 decarboxylation, B2/NAD-FAD redox, B3 NAD, B6 transamination, B12 methyl transfers, folate one-carbon, C antioxidant-collagen, A vision, D calcium, E membrane antioxidant, K clotting factors) make trace organics run metabolism - deficiencies (beriberi, scurvy, rickets, night blindness, pernicious anaemia) map missing coenzyme roles. Fat-soluble (A/D/E/K store, overdose possible) versus water-soluble (B/C excrete, need steady supply) split handling.
NEET Snapshot:
  • B-complex coenzymes run metabolism; A/D/E/K specialise.
  • Deficiencies map missing coenzyme roles precisely.

B1/B2/B3Decarboxylation, redox carriers
B12/folateMethyl, one-carbon transfers

A/D/E/KVision, calcium, membranes, clotting
NEET Practice MCQ
1

Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome (alcoholics) is deficiency of vitamin

Solution: Thiamine-dependent decarboxylation fails in brain metabolism.
Example 1.

Q. Night blindness, scurvy, beriberi: match vitamins and roles.

  1. Night blindness: vitamin A (retinal vision pigment).
  2. Scurvy: vitamin C (collagen crosslinking fails, gums bleed).
  3. Beriberi: B1 thiamine (carbohydrate metabolism stalls).
  4. Deficiency maps missing coenzyme roles.

Answer: A-vision, C-collagen, B1-energy metabolism.

Chapter 7 · Topic 15

Chemical structure of DNA

BiomoleculesBiomolecules and Practical ChemistryE. Nucleic acidsStep-by-step Topic

Topic in Depth

DNA structure (Watson-Crick antiparallel double helix: sugar-phosphate backbones outside, A=T double plus G triple C inside, 10 bp per 3.4 nm turn, major-minor grooves binding proteins) stores heredity stably - semiconservative replication copies, transcription reads, repair proofreads. Hershey-Chase proved DNA (not protein) carries genes; Franklin X-ray plus model-building solved the helix; sequencing reads billions of bases routinely.
NEET Snapshot:
  • Antiparallel helix with complementary pairing grooves.
  • Replication copies, transcription reads, repair proofreads.
Remember
  • Major groove reads sequences; proteins bind there.

Solution: Ten stacked pairs rise 3.4 nm per helical turn.

  • Choose intermediate: planar carbocation (rearranges), pyramidal carbanion (basic), radical chain, benzyne under harsh base, enol or enolate for alpha-chemistry.
  • Apply conditions: aqueous vs alcoholic KOH, bulky base for Hofmann, polar-protic for SN1/E1, polar-aprotic for SN2/E2, PCC to stop at aldehyde and dichromate to reach the acid.
  • Check selectivity: regioselectivity (where), stereoselectivity (inversion, racemisation, syn or anti) and chemoselectivity (which group reacts first).
Example 1.

Q. Two substrates on “DNA and RNA” differ by one substituent. Decide the major product.

  1. Draw both possible intermediates and count stabilising factors (resonance greater than hyperconjugation greater than +I).
  2. Apply the -I distance rule (alpha much greater than beta) and the +M ortho-para rule for aromatics.
  3. The lower-energy path is major; state the condition that reverses it (bulky base, peroxide, or solvent change).

Answer: the more stabilised intermediate and more substituted product wins; give the one-line reason.

Example 2 (NEET test pattern).

Q. Use the classic test for this family (Lucas, Tollens/Fehling, iodoform, bromine water, Baeyer, AgNO3 after fusion, or 2,4-DNP).

  1. Recall exact reagent, temperature and observation (colour or precipitate).
  2. Link observation to structure: aldehyde gives silver mirror; methyl ketone gives yellow CHI3; 3-degree alcohol gives immediate Lucas turbidity.
  3. Eliminate options by molecular formula first, then by functional-group test.

Answer: reagent gives observation gives structural conclusion.

Common mistakes.
  • Confusing R/S with + or - rotation; SN1 gives partial (not perfect) racemisation.
  • Expecting SN2 on a tertiary halide, or Cannizzaro on an aldehyde with alpha-H.
  • Forgetting that ketones resist mild oxidation and phenol gives no NaHCO3 effervescence.
